scope: Introductory definitions and notation for reading the collection. Finite examples are identified explicitly. Each work retains its own definitions, hypotheses and evidence status.

background.papers: Vectors, matrices, linear maps, kernels and images, and reading a statement with hypotheses. Consult the selected paper for any additional algebra or analysis it uses.
background.monographs: Begin with the introduction and glossary. Then use the volume's own definitions to identify the background needed for its subject.
background.research: Read the problem statement, recorded scope and open questions first. The program's definitions determine its subject prerequisites.
background.packages: Basic command-line use and the package's programming language. Check its platform requirements before installation.
background.experiments: Basic programming and familiarity with the stated data and evaluation method. Read the input limits and acceptance criteria before interpreting output.

glossary.definition: A way to represent a declared system using concrete spaces and operations while respecting its required relations. A finite matrix realization assigns a space to each type and a matrix to each permitted arrow.
Initial generating data from which the allowed operator action produces further elements. Whether a seed is sufficient depends on both the object and the declared action.
glossary.example_text: On R², let N(a,b) = (b,0) and v = (0,1). Then Nv = (1,0), so v and its image generate every vector by linear combinations.

glossary.definition: A label for a legal operator path or a packet coordinate. Examples include signal phases, residue classes, and positions in a packet tree. An address identifies a location in a representation, not necessarily a physical location.
A linear operator P satisfying P² = P. Applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once. This algebraic definition does not require orthogonality.
glossary.example_text: On R², P₁(a,b) = (a,0). Applying P₁ again still gives (a,0), so P₁² = P₁.

glossary.definition: In the finite projector example, a selected component Pᵢx or the subspace in which it lies, according to context. Signal, algebraic and arithmetic works may assign the word more specific meanings.
glossary.example_text: For x = (2,3)ᵀ, the coordinate projectors give packets P₁x = (2,0)ᵀ and P₂x = (0,3)ᵀ. Their sum recovers x.

glossary.definition: Values describing an object relative to a chosen representation. Coordinates can be unique basis coefficients or redundant measurements, depending on the setup.
glossary.example_text: The coordinate change C(a,b) = (a + b/2,b) sends x = (2,3)ᵀ to y = (7/2,3)ᵀ. These describe the same object in two coordinate systems.

glossary.definition: Analysis sends an object to coordinates. Synthesis returns an object from coordinates. In the finite linear model, A and S are linear maps and exact reconstruction is the identity SA = I.
glossary.example_text: The analysis A(a,b) = (a,b,a+b) sends (2,3)ᵀ to (2,3,5)ᵀ. The example’s synthesis S returns (2,3)ᵀ, with SA = I₂.

glossary.definition: The part of an operation connecting a source component to a target component. With source projector Pᵢ, target projector Qⱼ and operator T, the block is QⱼTPᵢ. Complete source and target families allow the blocks to reconstruct T.
glossary.example_text: For T = [[1,2],[3,4]], the coordinate block P₁TP₂ sends (2,3)ᵀ to (6,0)ᵀ. It carries source coordinate 2 into target coordinate 1.

glossary.definition: A compatible move from a coarser description to a finer one. In finite packet refinement, each fine packet has a coarse parent and each coarse projector is the sum of its children.
glossary.example_text: The zero-based even indices split into residue classes 0 and 2 modulo 4. Their selectors satisfy P₀ = F₀ + F₂.

glossary.definition: A discrepancy computed for a specified identity or reconstruction. In Example 5 it is r = x − x̂. Other operations may use a different sign or norm, so the definition belongs with the reported number.
glossary.example_text: Dropping residue class 2 modulo 4 from (1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8) gives r = (0,0,3,0,0,0,7,0). Its squared Euclidean norm is 58.

glossary.definition: An identified reason a requested construction cannot meet its stated conditions. In the recovery example, two inputs have the same coarse value but require different answers, so no recovery function from that value alone exists.
glossary.note: A nonzero numerical residual is not automatically a proof that every possible construction fails.
glossary.example_text: The inputs (1,0) and (0,1) have the same sum but different first coordinates. No function of their sum alone can return the first coordinate for every real input.

glossary.definition: A structured report describing a particular check, with its evidence class, residuals, and assumptions. The producer determines what was checked. A saved certificate describes a past calculation and needs revalidation for a new one.

Computed or stated in exact algebra or arithmetic under the declared hypotheses. Exact rational arithmetic avoids rounding of those rational values. It does not establish an unchecked modeling assumption.

Computed with finite-precision arithmetic and interpreted using a stated error or residual rule. A zero observed floating-point residual does not turn the whole computation into an exact-arithmetic proof.
A result that retains explicitly listed assumptions. In a computation record, some of those assumptions may not have been established by the computation. Passing its checks does not discharge them.

A recorded connection between a written claim and a formal Lean statement. Compare hypotheses, the full formal type, source edition, and execution record. A similar declaration name or a working link alone does not establish the correspondence.
A number from the declared coefficient field, used to multiply vectors. The hand-worked matrix examples use real scalars and exact rational entries.
glossary.quick_example: In 3(2,−1) = (6,−3), the number 3 is the scalar.

glossary.definition: A number system with addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by every nonzero element. The rational, real, and complex numbers are examples. A result over one field does not automatically hold over another.
An element of a vector space. In the finite examples it is a column of numbers. Its coordinates depend on a chosen representation.
glossary.quick_example: The pair (2,3) and the polynomial 2+3x are vectors in different declared vector spaces.

glossary.definition: A collection of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication, with the usual distributive and associative laws. The space of pairs of real numbers is denoted R².
glossary.quick_example: Pairs (x,y) with x+y = 0 form a vector space; pairs with x+y = 1 do not contain zero.

glossary.definition: A map T satisfying T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v) for all vectors u, v and allowed scalars a, b. A linear map preserves linear combinations.
glossary.quick_example: T(x,y) = (x+2y,3x) is linear. Adding a fixed nonzero offset would make it affine.

glossary.definition: A rectangular array representing a linear map after bases have been chosen. An m by n matrix takes n coordinates to m coordinates. Each output coordinate is a row multiplied by the input column.
The map I that leaves every input unchanged, so Ix = x. The subscript in I₂ or I₃ specifies the dimension when needed.
glossary.quick_example: I₂(2,3) = (2,3). The identity is different from a matrix with every entry equal to one.

glossary.definition: All finite linear combinations of a specified set of vectors. The span of the empty set consists only of the zero vector. With an operator action, one may first apply allowed operators and then take the span.
glossary.quick_example: The span of (1,1) is the line {(a,a) : a is a scalar}.

glossary.definition: A family is linearly independent when the only linear combination giving zero has every coefficient zero. No member of a finite independent family can be formed from the others.
glossary.quick_example: (1,0) and (0,1) are independent, while (1,0) and (2,0) are dependent.

glossary.definition: A linearly independent spanning family. Every vector has a unique finite linear combination in that basis. Redundant measurements can describe a vector without forming a basis.
glossary.quick_example: In the basis {(1,1),(1,−1)}, the vector (4,2) has coefficients (3,1).

glossary.definition: The number of vectors in a basis of a finite-dimensional vector space. In these examples, R² has dimension two even when three redundant measurements are stored.
glossary.quick_example: The subspace spanned by (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) has dimension two inside R³.

glossary.definition: For a linear map T, the vectors sent to zero: ker T = {x : Tx = 0}. A nonzero kernel describes directions that this map cannot distinguish from zero.
glossary.example_text: For the sum map R(a,b) = a+b over R, the vector (1,−1)ᵀ lies in the kernel: R(1,−1) = 0. Adding this vector does not change the observed sum.
glossary.quick_example: For R(x,y) = x+y, the kernel is span{(1,−1)}.

glossary.definition: The outputs actually attained by a map. For a linear map T, im T = {Tx : x is an allowed input} is a subspace of the target. The declared target can be larger than the image.
glossary.example_text: For A(a,b) = (a,b,a+b), the image consists of triples whose third coordinate is the sum of the first two. The coordinate vector (0,0,1)ᵀ lies outside it.
glossary.quick_example: The map x ↦ (x,0) has image the horizontal axis, even if its codomain is all of R².

glossary.definition: For a finite linear map, the dimension of its image. A matrix has full column rank when its columns are linearly independent, so it has no nonzero input in its kernel.
glossary.note: Matrix rank and seed rank answer different questions.
glossary.quick_example: The matrix [[1,1],[2,2]] has rank one because its second row and column add no independent direction.

glossary.definition: For real vector spaces, a symmetric bilinear pairing with ⟨v,v⟩ > 0 for every nonzero v. It defines lengths and angles. Positive weights give the pairing sum_i w_i u_i v_i. Complex inner products use conjugate symmetry and conjugate linearity in one argument.
glossary.quick_example: For u = (1,2), the weighted inner product with weights (1,3) gives ⟨u,u⟩ = 1+12 = 13.

glossary.definition: A nonnegative measure of size that is zero only at the zero vector, scales by the absolute value of a scalar and satisfies the triangle inequality. The Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates.
glossary.quick_example: The Euclidean norm of (3,4) is 5, while its 1-norm is 7.

glossary.definition: A system that records which objects an operation accepts and returns. A path of operations is legal only when consecutive input and output types agree. Types are part of the mathematical specification.
In the finite linear setting, a collection of linear operators closed under sums, scalar multiples, and composition. When a unital algebra is intended, the identity operator is included.

In the finite linear example, the least number of seeds whose operator-generated span is the whole space. More general definitions can involve modules, dense generation, and cardinalities. Read the definition in the chosen work.
glossary.example_text: For N(a,b) = (b,0) on R², one seed v = (0,1) suffices. With only the zero operator and the identity, two seeds are needed on the same space.

glossary.definition: For a single linear operator T, a vector v is cyclic when v, Tv, T²v and further iterates span the space under consideration. One cyclic vector is enough to generate that operator module.

A projector onto a subspace whose residual x − Px is perpendicular to that subspace in the specified inner product. In ordinary real Euclidean coordinates its matrix is symmetric as well as idempotent.
glossary.note: Orthogonality depends on the inner product. Weighted averaging need not have a symmetric matrix in ordinary coordinates.
glossary.example_text: With weights (1,3,2), the averaging map sends (2,6,9)ᵀ to (5,5,9)ᵀ. Its residual (−3,1,0)ᵀ has weighted inner product −3a + 3a = 0 with every retained vector (a,a,b)ᵀ. The averaging matrix is not symmetric in ordinary coordinates.

glossary.definition: In these finite examples, projectors Pᵢ with PᵢPⱼ = 0 for distinct indices and sum_i Pᵢ = I. These identities decompose every vector as x = sum_i Pᵢx.
The relation PᵢPⱼ = 0 whenever i and j differ. Applying one selection after a different selection gives zero. For a pair of projectors, both orders must be checked.
A subspace W preserved by an operator T, meaning T(W) is contained in W. Preservation does not require T to act as the identity on W.

A transformation between descriptions of the same object. In the invertible linear example the convention is y = Cx, so x = C⁻¹y. Keeping track of the direction prevents inverse formulas from being swapped.
A map that undoes another map in both directions. For a square invertible matrix C, the inverse satisfies C⁻¹C = CC⁻¹ = I.

For A mapping an input space to a coordinate space, S is a left inverse when SA = I on the input space. This gives exact reconstruction of analyzed inputs. It does not imply AS = I on the entire coordinate space.
glossary.example_text: The redundant-coordinate example has SA = I₂ but AS ≠ I₃. S recovers every original vector even though it does not invert every three-coordinate input.

glossary.definition: A representation containing more coordinate entries than are needed for a basis description. Valid coordinate lists can satisfy relations, such as a third measurement being the sum of the first two.
glossary.note: The reconstruction components SEᵢA can sum to the identity without being projectors.

glossary.definition: Applying one map after another. In a matrix product UT, T acts first and U acts second. The intermediate dimensions or types must agree.
The change in an operator matrix under an invertible coordinate change. With y = Cx and original operator T, the new matrix is CTC⁻¹. This usage is distinct from complex conjugation.
A linear map C connecting operators T and U by CT = UC. Applying T and then C agrees with applying C and then U. An intertwiner need not be invertible.
Passing to a description that groups or forgets distinctions. Combining fine packets can recover a coarse packet, while discarding the fine values can prevent later reconstruction.

For a sequence x and a positive integer m, the phase r collects samples x_(mk+r), with 0 ≤ r < m. Interleaving all phases reconstructs the indexed sequence. Filtering requires additional boundary and convention choices.
Integers with the same remainder modulo a positive integer m. Two integers belong to the same class when their difference is a multiple of m. Even and odd indices are the two classes modulo two.
Agreement between specified maps, operations or levels of a construction. The relevant equality must be stated, such as a coarse projector equaling the sum of its fine children.
A diagram in which the declared routes between the same starting and ending objects give the same map. In Example 3 the equality is D_y C = C D.
Recovering an object from its representation under the stated identities. Exact reconstruction may use all packet components or a synthesis map. Dropping components generally introduces a residual.
For a map R and an output s, the set of all inputs with R(x) = s. A proposed observation can be recovered from R(x) alone only if it is constant on each fiber.
glossary.example_text: For R(a,b) = a+b on R², the fiber over 1 consists of all (t,1−t) with real t. It contains both (1,0) and (0,1).

glossary.definition: Writing one map F as G composed with another map R, so F(x) = G(R(x)). This means the intermediate value R(x) contains enough information for the requested output F(x).
An object at a finer or richer level that maps to a specified object at a coarser level. Existence, uniqueness and compatibility of lifts are separate questions.

For positive weights and a finite partition, replace each value by its group’s weighted mean. The resulting map fixes group-constant vectors and is an orthogonal projector in the corresponding weighted inner product.

A construction that adds or realizes limits or missing structure under a specified mathematical definition. There is no single universal completion operation across the collection. A finite compatible tower does not by itself construct an infinite limit.
glossary.note: Mathematical completion and the editorial completion stage of a paper are different uses of the word.

glossary.definition: The capacity of a numerical representation. For the binary model here it is the number of significant binary digits, including the leading bit. More precision does not alone prove that an algorithm or its input is accurate.
A rational number expressible as an integer divided by a power of two. These are precisely the rational numbers with a finite binary expansion, apart from representation range limits.

Choosing a representable stored value for an exact value according to a specified rule. Nearest, ties to even chooses the closer value and resolves an exact midpoint by the parity of the last retained significand bit.

A unit in the last retained place at a specified precision and exponent. In the three-bit example the spacing in [1, 2) is 1/4, while the spacing in [2, 4) is 1/2. It is not one fixed absolute distance.

A numerical return whose sign compares the stored result with the exact value under the operation’s contract. Zero means exact, negative means below and positive means above. An error sentinel is not a numerical direction.

A declared threshold used by a numerical acceptance rule. Its units, scaling and comparison must match the residual being checked. A residual below tolerance is evidence within that rule, not exact equality in general.
An assumption required by a statement or construction. It may describe the space, arithmetic, domain, regularity or supplied data. A conclusion applies only where its hypotheses hold.
A mathematical statement established by a proof from its specified assumptions. A theorem may be conditional on explicit hypotheses, even when the implication itself is fully proved.

An argument establishing a statement from its hypotheses and accepted prior results. A worked input illustrates a statement. A general identity or argument is needed to establish a claim about every allowed input.
A method for discovery, search or estimation without a complete guarantee for the claimed outcome. Its suggestions can lead to later proofs or checks, but the suggestions alone do not establish them.

A check over specified, finitely many inputs or cases. Exhaustive checking can prove a claim about that finite domain. Sampling a larger domain does not establish the universal claim without an additional argument.
A subset of a vector space that contains zero and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Kernels and images of linear maps are subspaces.
glossary.quick_example: The plane z = 0 in R³ is a subspace; the parallel plane z = 1 is not.

glossary.definition: The dimension of the kernel of a finite-dimensional linear map. It counts independent input directions erased by the map.
glossary.example_text: For T(x₁,x₂,x₃) = (x₁+x₂,x₂+x₃), the kernel is span{(−1,1,−1)ᵀ}. It has one free direction, so nullity T = 1.
glossary.quick_example: The map R(x,y,z) = x+y has kernel {(a,−a,b)}, so its nullity is two.

glossary.definition: For a linear map with finite-dimensional domain V, dim V = rank T + nullity T. The rank concerns the image, not the dimension of the entire declared target.
glossary.example_text: The map T(x₁,x₂,x₃) = (x₁+x₂,x₂+x₃) has rank two and a one-dimensional kernel. Its three-dimensional domain therefore satisfies 3 = 2 + 1 = rank T + nullity T.
glossary.quick_example: For R(x,y,z) = x+y, domain dimension 3 equals rank 1 plus nullity 2.

glossary.definition: A map that sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs. A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel contains only zero.
glossary.quick_example: The map x ↦ (x,2x) is injective, although it does not reach every pair.

glossary.definition: A map whose image is its entire declared target. Surjectivity depends on which target is specified.
glossary.quick_example: The map (x,y) ↦ x reaches every real number, although many pairs have the same output.

glossary.definition: A bijective linear map between vector spaces over the same field. Its inverse is linear. It preserves the vector-space structure, although lengths need not be preserved.
A decomposition into subspaces in which each vector has a unique sum of components. For two subspaces, uniqueness is equivalent to their intersection containing only zero.
glossary.quick_example: Every pair (x,y) is uniquely (x,0)+(0,y), the sum of one vector from each coordinate axis.

glossary.definition: The vector space V/W obtained by identifying vectors whose difference lies in a subspace W. A coset x+W records the equivalence class of x.
glossary.quick_example: Modulo span{(1,−1)}, the pairs (2,3) and (4,1) represent the same class because their difference is (2,−2).

glossary.definition: A nonzero vector v for which Tv = λv. The scalar λ is the associated eigenvalue. Zero is excluded from the definition of eigenvector.
glossary.quick_example: For T = diag(2,3), the nonzero vector (1,0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2.

glossary.definition: A scalar λ such that Tv = λv for some nonzero v over the specified field. A real matrix may have no real eigenvalue even though it has eigenvalues over the complex numbers.
For an operator T and scalar λ, the kernel of T − λI. It includes zero and all eigenvectors with eigenvalue λ.
glossary.quick_example: For T = diag(2,2,3), the eigenvalue-2 eigenspace is the plane {(x,y,0)}.

glossary.definition: An operator that has a basis of eigenvectors over the stated field. Equivalently, its matrix becomes diagonal after an invertible change of basis.
Substitute T into p(t) = a₀ + a₁t + ⋯ + aₙtⁿ to obtain p(T) = a₀I + a₁T + ⋯ + aₙTⁿ. The constant term acts through the identity operator.
For a linear operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional space over a field, the monic polynomial of least degree with m(T) = 0. It records an exact operator relation.
glossary.quick_example: For T = diag(2,3), the minimal polynomial is (t−2)(t−3).

glossary.definition: In the diagonalizable finite example, the projector onto one eigenspace along the sum of the others. Distinct eigenvalues allow a polynomial interpolation formula for these projectors.
glossary.example_text: For T(a,b) = (2a+b,3b), the projectors P₂ = 3I−T and P₃ = T−2I split (2,3)ᵀ into (−1,0)ᵀ and (3,3)ᵀ. The identity T = 2P₂+3P₃ then gives T(2,3)ᵀ = (7,9)ᵀ.

glossary.definition: For operators on the same space, [A,B] = AB − BA. A zero commutator means the two orders of composition agree.
glossary.quick_example: For P = diag(1,0) and T swapping coordinates, PT−TP = [[0,1],[−1,0]].

glossary.definition: A matrix grouped into rectangular submatrices according to decompositions of its input and output coordinates. Block products require the inner dimensions to agree.
For the block matrix [[A,B],[C,D]] with invertible A, the Schur complement of A is D − CA⁻¹B. It is the remaining operator after eliminating the first block of unknowns.
glossary.quick_example: In [[2,1],[1,3]], eliminating the invertible upper-left entry gives the scalar complement 3−1/2 = 5/2.

glossary.definition: Removing selected unknowns by solving part of a system and substituting into the remaining equations. The substitution requires its stated invertibility or solvability assumptions.
A scalar attached to a square matrix. For [[a,b],[c,d]] it is ad − bc. Over a field, a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
glossary.quick_example: The matrix [[1,2],[3,4]] has determinant 4−6 = −2 and is invertible over the real numbers.

glossary.definition: The relation a ≡ b modulo m means m divides a − b, with m a positive integer. It compares residue classes, not the ordinary sizes of a and b.
glossary.quick_example: 17 and 2 are congruent modulo 5 because their difference 15 is divisible by 5.

glossary.definition: Integers with greatest common divisor one. Pairwise coprime moduli give independent residue coordinates in the ordinary Chinese remainder theorem.
glossary.quick_example: The integers 4 and 9 are coprime; 4 and 6 have common divisor 2.

glossary.definition: An integer b with ab ≡ 1 modulo m. For m greater than one, it exists exactly when a and m are coprime. The inverse is a residue class modulo m.
glossary.quick_example: The inverse of 3 modulo 7 is 5 because 3·5 = 15 is congruent to 1.

glossary.definition: For pairwise coprime positive moduli, a tuple of residues specifies exactly one residue class modulo their product. Selecting an integer representative requires an additional convention.
glossary.quick_example: The requirements x ≡ 1 modulo 2 and x ≡ 2 modulo 3 give x ≡ 5 modulo 6.

glossary.definition: A two-sample transform that separates an average and a difference. The tutorial uses a = (u+v)/2 and d = (u−v)/2, with inverse (u,v) = (a+d,a−d). Other Haar normalizations use square roots.
In the Haar pair example, the signed half-difference d = (u−v)/2. It records the information lost when the pair is replaced by its repeated average.
A real square matrix Q with QᵀQ = QQᵀ = I. It preserves the Euclidean inner product and norm. A transform with orthogonal rows can still need normalization to satisfy this identity.
A declared scaling convention. For a Haar pair, dividing sums and differences by two gives averages, while dividing by √2 gives a Euclidean norm-preserving transform.
A sequence of arrows in which each output type matches the next input type. Its realization is the corresponding ordered composition. An empty path at a type acts as its identity.
A required equality between legal operator expressions, such as T² = 0. In a typed system, both sides must have the same input and output types.
The declared input and target spaces of a map. The codomain includes all permitted outputs, while the image consists of outputs actually attained.
glossary.quick_example: For T: R² → R³ with T(x,y) = (x,y,0), the domain is R², codomain is R³ and image is a plane.

glossary.definition: The scalar multiplying a specified basis term. In f(z) = sum aₙzⁿ, aₙ is the coefficient of zⁿ.
glossary.quick_example: In 2+5x+3x², the coefficient of x is 5; in a different basis the coefficient list changes.

glossary.definition: An expression sum aₙzⁿ with infinitely many coefficient positions. A formal power series is manipulated through its coefficients. Evaluating it at a number additionally requires convergence.
Keeping only specified degrees or levels. Equality modulo zᴺ means the coefficients of degrees below N agree. It need not be equality of the full functions or series.

For a power series over a field with nonzero constant coefficient, the unique series whose product with it is one. Its coefficients are determined recursively. A finite truncation only verifies the corresponding finite set of coefficient identities.
aliases: Multiplicative inverse of a formal series
glossary.quick_example: The formal reciprocal of 1−z is 1+z+z²+⋯ because their Cauchy product is 1.

glossary.definition: The multiplication rule cₙ = sum from k=0 to n of aₖbₙ₋ₖ for ordinary power series. Each output coefficient is a finite sum, even when the series are infinite.

A complex number ω with ωᴺ = 1 for a positive integer N. It is primitive when N is its least positive such exponent. A weighted average over the powers of a primitive Nth root selects coefficients in one residue class modulo N.
glossary.quick_example: The number i has exact order 4: i⁴ = 1, and no smaller positive power equals 1.

glossary.definition: For real a and b, the conjugate of a+bi is a−bi. The squared modulus is (a+bi)(a−bi) = a²+b².
For a complex matrix in orthonormal bases, the adjoint A* is its conjugate transpose. In real orthonormal bases this is the ordinary transpose.
glossary.quick_example: The adjoint of [[1,i],[0,2]] is [[1,0],[−i,2]]. Both transposition and conjugation are required.

glossary.definition: A complex square matrix U with U*U = UU* = I. It preserves the complex inner product and therefore vector norms.
glossary.quick_example: diag(1,i) is unitary because its adjoint diag(1,−i) is its inverse.

glossary.definition: A complex coordinate of a normalized state vector in a chosen orthonormal basis. Its squared modulus gives that basis outcome’s probability. Relative phases can affect measurements in other bases.

A positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. A normalized vector ψ gives the pure-state matrix ρ = ψψ*. Different vectors that differ only by an overall complex phase give the same density matrix.
glossary.example_text: The normalized vector ψ = (3/5,4i/5)ᵀ gives ρ = ψψ*. Its diagonal entries are 9/25 and 16/25, its upper-right entry is −12i/25, and its lower-left entry is 12i/25. Its trace is one.

glossary.definition: The sum of diagonal entries of a square matrix. It is unchanged by an invertible change of basis. Field trace is a related arithmetic construction with its own definition.
For a density matrix ρ and an orthogonal measurement projector P, the outcome probability is tr(Pρ). A complete orthogonal projector family gives probabilities summing to one.
glossary.example_text: For ψ = (3/5,4i/5)ᵀ and ρ = ψψ*, the coordinate projectors P₀ = diag(1,0) and P₁ = diag(0,1) give tr(P₀ρ) = 9/25 and tr(P₁ρ) = 16/25. These probabilities sum to one.

glossary.definition: The number tr(ρ²). For a finite density matrix it equals one exactly for a pure state and is smaller for a mixed state.
glossary.example_text: For ρ = ψψ* with ψ = (3/5,4i/5)ᵀ, tr(ρ²) = 1. After coordinate dephasing, the purity is (9/25)² + (16/25)² = 337/625, which is less than one.

glossary.definition: For a specified complete orthogonal family Pᵢ, the channel ρ ↦ sum PᵢρPᵢ removes coherence between different selected subspaces. Its effect depends on the chosen decomposition.
glossary.example_text: The coordinate measurement with its outcome forgotten sends the example’s ρ to P₀ρP₀ + P₁ρP₁ = diag(9/25,16/25). The off-diagonal terms disappear while the two coordinate probabilities remain unchanged.

glossary.definition: Matrices Kᵢ describing a finite quantum channel by Φ(ρ) = sum KᵢρKᵢ*. The condition sum Kᵢ*Kᵢ = I makes this map trace preserving.
An integer pⁿ with p prime and n a nonnegative integer. Successive positive powers give the moduli in the lift-branch example.
Passing from a residue class modulo pⁿ⁺¹ to its class modulo pⁿ. This map forgets the highest retained base-p digit.
A sequence of solutions at successive levels whose reductions agree. A node at one finite level can have several children or no child.
A collection of objects with specified maps between levels and stated compatibility identities. For modular solutions, the next residue must reduce to the preceding one.
For a prime p, an element of the inverse limit of the residue rings modulo pⁿ. It specifies a compatible residue at every positive level. A finite list of residues is only a truncation of that data.
A branch reaches the chosen last level without losing compatibility or the required equations. Survival to that level alone says nothing about the next one.
glossary.example_text: The residue 9 solves x² ≡ 1 modulo 16. Its only candidate lifts modulo 32 are 9 and 25, and both squares equal 17 modulo 32. This branch reaches level four but has no child at level five.

glossary.definition: The smallest subfield of a field. In characteristic p it consists of the p scalar classes and is isomorphic to Fₚ. In characteristic zero it is isomorphic to the rational numbers.
glossary.quick_example: The field F₅ has five elements. Its nonzero element 2 has inverse 3.

glossary.definition: A field containing a specified smaller field. The extension degree is its vector-space dimension over that smaller field.
In a finite field of characteristic p, the map x ↦ xᵖ is an automorphism. Over F_q, the relative Frobenius is x ↦ x^q. The example uses q = p = 5.
glossary.example_text: In F₂₅ = F₅[α] with α² = 3, one has α⁵ = −α. Thus Frobenius sends 1+α to 1−α, and applying it twice returns 1+α.
glossary.quick_example: In characteristic p, (a+b)ᵖ = aᵖ+bᵖ. On Fₚ itself the Frobenius fixes every element.

glossary.definition: For a finite field extension L/K, the trace of the K-linear map that multiplies L by an element a. In F₂₅/F₅ it is a+a⁵.
For a finite field extension L/K, the determinant of multiplication by an element a as a K-linear map. In F₂₅/F₅ it is a·a⁵. This norm is algebraic and is not a vector length.
glossary.example_text: For β = 1+α in F₂₅ = F₅[α] with α² = 3, the norm to F₅ is ββ⁵ = (1+α)(1−α) = 1−3 = 3 in F₅.

glossary.definition: A nonconstant polynomial over a field that cannot be factored into two polynomials of positive degree over that field. For degree two, irreducibility is equivalent to having no root in the field.
A system with addition, subtraction and commutative multiplication satisfying the ring laws and having a multiplicative identity. A nonzero element need not have a multiplicative inverse.
glossary.quick_example: The integers form a commutative ring with identity, but 2 has no multiplicative inverse within the integers.

glossary.definition: An abelian additive group with a scalar action by a ring satisfying the usual distributive, associative, and identity laws. For a module over Q[t], multiplication by t can be specified by a Q-linear operator.
glossary.quick_example: An abelian group is a module over Z, where multiplying by an integer means repeated addition and its inverse.

glossary.definition: A description of a module by generators and relations. A finite matrix A: Rᵐ → Rⁿ presents the quotient Rⁿ/im A.
For a linear map or module map A: U → V, the quotient V/im A. It records target classes modulo those already reached by A.
glossary.quick_example: The cokernel of multiplication by 2 on Z is Z/2Z, which records the two parity classes.

glossary.definition: An operator N for which Nᵏ = 0 for some positive integer k. It can be nonzero. The smallest such k on a nonzero space is its nilpotency index.
glossary.quick_example: N = [[0,1],[0,0]] is nonzero, but N² = 0.

glossary.definition: The ideal of ring elements that act as zero on every element of a module. For Q[t]/(tᵏ), the annihilator is the ideal (tᵏ).
glossary.quick_example: In the Z-module Z/6Z, every multiple of 6 acts as zero, so its annihilator is the ideal (6).

glossary.definition: The prime ideals at which a module’s localization is nonzero. In the example Q[t]/(tᵏ), the support is the single prime ideal (t). The underlying support set does not determine k or the module.
glossary.example_text: Over R = Q[t], the modules R/(t) and R/(t²) both have support {(t)}. Their rational dimensions are one and two, so equal support does not identify the modules.

glossary.definition: For a finite presentation Rᵐ → Rⁿ → M → 0 over a commutative ring, the ideal generated by the n by n minors of the presentation matrix. In the one-generator example with relation tᵏ, it is (tᵏ).

For Q[t]/(tᵏ) supported at t=0, the integer k records the module’s length and its Q-vector-space dimension. This is additional data beyond the one-point support set. Other works use multiplicity with their own specified objects.
glossary.example_text: The module Q[t]/(t²) has basis (1,t) over Q and multiplicity two in this example. Its fiber at t = 0 still has dimension one. That special-fiber dimension does not recover the full module’s rational dimension.

glossary.definition: A complex square matrix A with A* = A. Its diagonal entries are real and opposite off-diagonal entries are complex conjugates. This condition alone does not imply positivity.
glossary.quick_example: The matrix [[1,i],[−i,2]] is Hermitian because conjugating and transposing returns it.

glossary.definition: A Hermitian matrix A for which v*Av is nonnegative for every vector v. Zero eigenvalues are allowed.
glossary.quick_example: [[1,1],[1,1]] is positive semidefinite because its quadratic form is |x+y|², and it has a nonzero kernel.

glossary.definition: Off-diagonal density-matrix entries that encode relations between different basis components. They can contribute to probabilities after a change of measurement basis.
An additive subgroup of a commutative ring closed under multiplication by every element of the ring. The principal ideal (f) consists of all multiples of f.
glossary.quick_example: The even integers form the ideal (2) in Z: multiplying an even integer by any integer stays even.

glossary.definition: A proper ideal P such that ab in P implies a in P or b in P. The ideal (t) in Q[t] is prime because the quotient is the field Q.

A construction that makes ring elements outside a chosen prime ideal invertible, and carries a module along with that scalar change. The prime lies in the module’s support exactly when the localized module is nonzero.
A declared finite collection of claim nodes, admissible leaves, and recorded inference rules. Certificate validity is relative to this supplied system.
A node allowed as a starting point under the declared proof-field contract. Selecting such a leaf does not require deriving it again inside that certificate.
A specified set of premise nodes together with a conclusion node. The certificate can use the rule only when the required premises have been derived and its recorded certification permits it.
The nodes obtainable by admitting selected admissible leaves and repeatedly applying the retained certified rules whose premises are available.
A valid node-and-rule certificate with no valid strictly smaller subcertificate under componentwise inclusion. Several incomparable minimal certificates can exist.
glossary.example_text: The certificate built from leaves s₁ and s₃ derives a, b, c and d, then the target t. Removing either selected leaf or any of its five retained rules breaks that derivation, so this certificate is inclusion-minimal.

glossary.definition: A certificate contained componentwise in every certificate for the same request and rule system. This is stronger than being inclusion-minimal or having minimum numerical cost.
glossary.example_text: The two optimal certificates start from {s₁,s₃} and {s₂,s₄}. Their intersection contains no admissible leaf. With no mandatory starting leaves, it cannot derive t, so there is no least certificate in this rule system.

glossary.definition: A valid certificate attaining the lowest declared total cost among the permitted certificates. Costs count selected items according to the supplied rule, so a shared premise need not be charged each time it is used.
glossary.example_text: Each selected leaf costs one and supplies two of four required obligations. Either pair {s₁,s₃} or {s₂,s₄} reaches the target at cost two, while zero or one leaf cannot. Reusing a selected leaf for two consequences does not double its cost.

glossary.definition: The state coordinates or summary retained for a specified prediction task. A visible value need not contain enough information to determine its own next value.
The part of the declared full state omitted by the current observation or summary. It can influence later visible outputs even when it does not affect the current output.
An initialization that fixes the hidden coordinates by a specified rule. The example uses R(y)=(y,0). Results for this preparation need not hold for arbitrary hidden starting values.

For the block update (y,z) ↦ (Ay+Bz,Gy+Dz), the maps Mₖ=BDᵏG describe a visible-to-hidden entry, k hidden transitions, and a return. The first effect of Mₖ on prepared visible evolution occurs after k+2 full steps.
glossary.example_text: For A = B = G = 1 and D = 0 in the visible and hidden block update, M₀ = BD⁰G = 1 while Mₖ = 0 for k ≥ 1. Information entering the hidden coordinate returns after two full steps.

glossary.definition: A transition rule determined by the retained current state, under the declared controls and initialization contract. For deterministic maps, full states with the same summary must have the same next summary.
Enlarging a retained state with additional coordinates or history needed for future prediction. The hidden-memory example retains the previous visible value along with the current one.
The identity Eₘ₊ₙ=EₘEₙ for nonnegative step counts, with E₀ the identity. It expresses agreement between uninterrupted evolution and successive uses of the same state-level evolution maps.
glossary.example_text: With the hidden coordinate initialized to zero, the prepared visible maps Eₙ = CTⁿR are scalar multipliers with E₁ = 1 and E₂ = 2. Thus E₂ ≠ E₁E₁. Restarting from the visible value resets hidden information.

glossary.definition: Supplied input-output pairs for an unknown operation. For a linear operation, every linear relation among calibrated inputs must be respected by the supplied outputs.
The span of the calibrated input vectors. Consistent exact linear calibration determines the operation on this span. Its outputs can leave that span.
glossary.example_text: The measurements Te₁ = e₁ and Te₂ = e₃ determine T(ae₁+be₂) = ae₁+be₃ throughout U = span(e₁,e₂). In particular, T(2e₁−e₂) = 2e₁−e₃, while Te₃ remains unspecified.

glossary.definition: A model satisfying all supplied data and every declared structural assumption. In the calibration example, all linear extensions of the known restriction are allowed, and each model stays fixed through a trajectory.
A linear map on a larger vector space that agrees with a given map on its original subspace. Values on an added basis can vary unless further conditions are imposed.

For the tutorial’s unrestricted linear extension class and full-state output, the largest subspace inside the calibration span preserved by every calibrated operation. All finite operation sequences from this subspace are determined by the calibration.
glossary.example_text: With Te₁ = e₁ and Te₂ = e₃, the known image of ae₁+be₂ stays in U = span(e₁,e₂) exactly when b = 0. The retained domain stabilizes at span(e₁), where every compatible extension satisfies Tⁿ(ae₁) = ae₁ for all n ≥ 0.

glossary.term: Identifiability relative to a model class
glossary.definition: A requested quantity is identifiable from the supplied data when every compatible model gives the same value. Identifying a particular output can require less information than identifying the whole model.
glossary.quick_example: Observing only x+y cannot distinguish parameter pairs (1,2) and (2,1) if both are allowed.

glossary.definition: For n≥1, differentiating a power-series term aₙzⁿ gives n aₙzⁿ⁻¹. Constant terms differentiate to zero. Formal differentiation acts on coefficients. An analytic interpretation uses the function’s convergence and differentiability conditions.
An equation relating an unknown function to one or more of its derivatives. The example also evaluates the same function at contracted arguments qz and rz.
A specified value, or collection of derivative values, used with a differential equation. The feedback example fixes T(0)=0, and the equation then forces T′(0)=1.
Evaluation at qz with 0<q<1 in the feedback example. A term cₙzⁿ becomes cₙqⁿzⁿ after this substitution. The scaling is inside the defining equation.

A rule determining successive series coefficients from earlier ones. It gives exact finite calculations at each degree. Analytic convergence and bounds for a discarded tail require additional arguments.
An allowed vector added to the span of the original image so that a required target can become reachable. Both the target equation and the permitted coefficient system must remain specified.

A repair problem allowing freely chosen added directions over the declared field. In the rational finite-dimensional setting, the minimum added dimension is the dimension of the span of the target residual classes in the original cokernel.
A supplied finite list of candidate directions, with costs and any selection restrictions. Feasibility and optimality are judged using this list and the original target equation.
The declared cost of the selected repair choices. In the tutorial it is the sum of their selection costs, paid once per choice, independently of the rational coefficients used to combine them.
Existence of a solution satisfying the stated equations and admissibility conditions. Failure of one candidate or exhaustion of a search budget does not by itself show infeasibility.
A linear functional that annihilates every allowed direction but has a nonzero value on the required target. It proves that this target lies outside their span under the stated linear problem.

A model with a Gaussian state and specified linear observations with Gaussian noise. The tutorial supplies an independent noise variable, a prior mean and covariance, an observation matrix and a positive noise variance.
The state distribution specified before conditioning on the observation under the declared model. A Gaussian prior is described by its mean and covariance.

For a fixed observed value, the observation density viewed as a function of the proposed state or parameter. It is combined with the prior and normalized to obtain a posterior density when that density formula applies.
The state distribution conditional on the observed data under the supplied prior and observation model. The tutorial computes the usual explicit Gaussian conditional density by completing the square.
For a random vector X with mean m and finite second moments, the matrix E[(X−m)(X−m)ᵀ]. Its diagonal entries are variances. For a unit direction u, uᵀCu is the variance in that direction.
glossary.quick_example: Independent coordinates with variances 1 and 4 have covariance matrix diag(1,4).

glossary.definition: The inverse covariance when the covariance is invertible. In a nonsingular Gaussian density it appears in the quadratic exponent. This use of precision is distinct from the number of bits in stored arithmetic.
glossary.quick_example: For covariance diag(1,4), the precision matrix is diag(1,1/4).

glossary.definition: The difference d=y−Hm between an observation and its predicted mean in the linear model. Its covariance is S=HPHᵀ+R when the state covariance is P and the independent noise covariance is R.
glossary.quick_example: If an observation is 7 and the predicted observation is 5, the innovation is 2 under the observation-minus-prediction convention.

glossary.definition: For the declared linear Gaussian model, K=PHᵀ(HPHᵀ+R)⁻¹. Multiplying the innovation by K gives the posterior mean correction. Positive noise covariance makes the displayed observation-space inverse exist.

For a gain B, the matrix (I−BH)P(I−BH)ᵀ+BRBᵀ. It is positive semidefinite for valid prior and noise covariances. At the exact gain it equals the posterior covariance. A general gain still needs its own accuracy check.
A specified rule T:X→Y taking each allowed input to an output of the declared type. The word alone does not imply linearity, invertibility, or continuity. Those are additional properties of the rule.
glossary.example_text: R(x₁,x₂)=x₁+x₂ maps a pair to a scalar, while B(s)=(s,0) maps a scalar to a pair. Thus RB and BR act on different spaces.

glossary.definition: A map between vector spaces of the form x↦Lx+c, where L is linear and c is a fixed output vector. The translation c may move zero, so the map is linear exactly when c=0.
glossary.example_text: The rule A(x₁,x₂)=2x₁−x₂+3 is affine. Its linear part is L(x₁,x₂)=2x₁−x₂, and A(0,0)=3.
glossary.quick_example: f(x) = 2x+1 is affine; f(0) = 1 shows it is not linear.

glossary.definition: A map between vector spaces that does not satisfy the linear-combination identity for all allowed vectors and scalars. Splitting its input into packets need not split its output into the sum of the separate packet outputs.
glossary.example_text: For f(x₁,x₂)=x₁x₂, f(1,0)+f(0,1)=0 but f((1,0)+(0,1))=1. The two input directions interact.

glossary.definition: For R:X→S, a map B:S→X satisfying RB=I on S. It chooses an input that produces each summary value. This identity does not require BR=I on X.
glossary.example_text: For R(x₁,x₂)=x₁+x₂ and B(s)=(s,0), RB(s)=s. But BR(0,1)=(1,0), so this choice does not recover every original pair.
glossary.quick_example: For R(x,y) = x, the map S(x) = (x,0) satisfies RS = I. The reverse product SR deletes the second coordinate.

glossary.definition: For linear maps A:X→X′ and B:Y→Y′, the linear map A⊗B determined by (A⊗B)(x⊗y)=Ax⊗By. Choosing bases represents it by a Kronecker matrix on the tensor-product coordinates.
glossary.example_text: With A=diag(2,3) and B the two-coordinate swap, A⊗B sends (1,2,0,0)ᵀ to (4,2,0,0)ᵀ. It acts on four coordinates, while AB acts on two.

glossary.definition: A linear projector whose range and kernel are complementary but not perpendicular in the chosen inner product. It reconstructs by x=Px+(I−P)x, while the two pieces need not give an orthogonal energy decomposition.
glossary.example_text: P(x₁,x₂)=(x₁+x₂,0) splits (2,3)ᵀ as (5,0)ᵀ+(−3,3)ᵀ. Their squared Euclidean lengths sum to 43, although the original squared length is 13.

glossary.definition: For a linear map between specified normed spaces with a nonzero domain, the supremum of ‖Tx‖/‖x‖ over nonzero inputs. It is the smallest uniform amplification bound when finite. The input and output norms are part of its meaning.
glossary.example_text: For E=[[0,2],[3,0]], the Euclidean induced norm is 3 because EᵀE=diag(9,4). Thus ‖Ex‖₂≤3‖x‖₂ for every input.
glossary.note: For the zero input space, the operator norm is defined to be zero.

glossary.term: Condition number of a coordinate map
glossary.definition: For an invertible linear coordinate map C on a nonzero finite-dimensional normed space, κ(C)=‖C‖‖C⁻¹‖. It bounds how the chosen coordinate representation can amplify errors, and depends on the norms being used.
glossary.example_text: C=[[1,10],[0,1]] and C⁻¹ both have infinity norm 11, so κ∞(C)=121. Conjugating diag(1,2) by C keeps its eigenvalues but changes its infinity norm from 2 to 11.
glossary.quick_example: For C = diag(1,100), κ₂(C) = 100. The map stretches one coordinate one hundred times more than the other.

glossary.definition: For an n by n complex matrix with n ≥ 1, the largest absolute value of its eigenvalues. For a real matrix, use its complex eigenvalues. This scalar need not equal the largest one-step amplification measured by an induced norm.
glossary.example_text: N=[[0,M],[0,0]] with M>0 has spectral radius zero and Euclidean operator norm M. Since N²=0, this large one-step gain disappears at the second power.

glossary.definition: For bounded linear maps Tₘ and T between fixed normed spaces, convergence Tₘx→Tx in the output norm for every fixed input x. It does not require one error bound to tend to zero uniformly over all unit inputs.
glossary.example_text: On ℓ², let Pₘ keep the first m coordinates. Then ‖x−Pₘx‖₂² is the tail sum of |xₖ|² and tends to zero for each fixed square-summable x.
glossary.note: The square-summable sequence space ℓ² consists of sequences x for which Σₖ|xₖ|² is finite.

glossary.definition: Convergence ‖Tₘ−T‖→0 for bounded linear maps between fixed normed spaces. It controls the error uniformly over all inputs of norm at most one, and implies strong operator convergence.
glossary.example_text: The first-m-coordinate projectors Pₘ on ℓ² converge strongly to I, but ‖I−Pₘ‖=1 for every finite m: a unit vector beyond the retained coordinates is still completely omitted.

glossary.definition: The polynomial b₀(x)=1 and bₖ(x)=x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1) for k≥1. These monic polynomials form a basis of the polynomial space. Falling degree records the basis index k, which need not match an ordinary-power packet after expansion.
glossary.example_text: b₃(x)=x³−3x²+2x, while x³=b₁(x)+3b₂(x)+b₃(x). The map Φ(zᵏ)=bₖ therefore has Φ⁻¹(x³)=z+3z²+z³.

glossary.definition: The operator Δf(x)=f(x+1)−f(x). On rational polynomials, Δbₖ=k bₖ₋₁ for the falling-factorial basis and Δb₀=0. Under Φ(zᵏ)=bₖ, this is the transported source derivative: Δ=ΦD_zΦ⁻¹.
aliases: Delta operator in the polynomial example
glossary.example_text: For f(x)=x³, Δf(x)=3x²+3x+1. Ordinary differentiation in x instead gives 3x², so the coordinate transport matters.

glossary.definition: On rational polynomials, the operator Af(x)=x f(x−1), which sends bₖ to bₖ₊₁. It is multiplication by the source variable transported through Φ(zᵏ)=bₖ, so A=Φ(z·)Φ⁻¹.
aliases: Raising operator in the polynomial example
glossary.example_text: A b₂=x(x−1)(x−2)=b₃. Together with Δbₖ=k bₖ₋₁, this gives (ΔA−AΔ)bₖ=bₖ.
glossary.note: The identity ΔA−AΔ=I is on the full polynomial space. A finite square truncation that drops the highest raised degree changes the boundary calculation.

glossary.definition: On rational polynomials, N=AΔ with A the falling-factorial raising operator. Explicitly, Nf(x)=x(f(x)−f(x−1)), and Nbₖ=k bₖ. Its eigenvalue records falling degree in this basis.
aliases: Degree operator in the falling-factorial basis
glossary.example_text: For b₃=x(x−1)(x−2), Nb₃=3b₃.
glossary.note: In positive characteristic, different degrees can give the same eigenvalue. Over F₃, b₀ and b₃ both have eigenvalue zero, so a polynomial in N cannot separate them.

glossary.definition: For an integer m≥2 and 0≤r<m, the projector Pᵣ retaining exactly the coefficients whose basis degree k satisfies k≡r modulo m. The basis is part of the definition. In falling-factorial coordinates the corresponding projector is Qᵣ=ΦPᵣΦ⁻¹.
glossary.example_text: For x³=b₁+3b₂+b₃, the even falling-degree packet is 3b₂ and the odd packet is b₁+b₃. At x=4 their values are 36 and 28, summing to 64.
glossary.note: Coefficient selection is defined over any commutative ring. Over a field, its roots-of-unity averaging formula requires a primitive mth root and invertible m.

glossary.definition: Given an invertible linear map Φ between two representations, the target product f⋆g=Φ(Φ⁻¹f·Φ⁻¹g), where · is the declared source product. This carries the source multiplication law into the target coordinates.
aliases: Star product in the polynomial example
glossary.example_text: For Φ(zᵏ)=bₖ, one has bₐ⋆bᵦ=bₐ₊ᵦ and x⋆x=x(x−1). The forward difference satisfies Δ(f⋆g)=(Δf)⋆g+f⋆(Δg).
glossary.note: Ordinary target multiplication is a different product: Δ(x²)=2x+1, whereas Δ(x⋆x)=2x.

glossary.definition: For a specified scalar shift h, the operator T_h f(x)=f(x+h). Over rational polynomials it is linear, with T₀=I and T_hT_k=T_{h+k}. In falling-factorial coordinates, a unit shift satisfies T₁=I+Δ.
glossary.example_text: For f=x³ and the even falling-degree projector Q₀, Q₀T₁f(4)=73 while T₁Q₀f(4)=60. Both orders translate the total correctly after all packets are added, but the individual packets differ.

glossary.definition: For f=Σₖaₖbₖ in the falling-factorial basis over Q, the coefficient is aₖ=Δᵏf(0)/k!. Repeated forward differences lower the basis index, and evaluation at zero isolates the matching coefficient.
glossary.example_text: The samples of x³ at 0,1,2,3 are 0,1,8,27. The first entries of successive difference rows are 0,1,6,6. Dividing by 0!,1!,2!,3! yields the coefficients 0,1,3,1.
glossary.note: This division formula requires the factorial denominators to be invertible. The integral Stirling basis change remains invertible over any commutative ring, even where this sampling formula fails.

glossary.definition: The declared set of inputs on which a construction or claim is required to work. Restricting this set can change fibers, recovery, and feasibility, so the input restriction belongs to the mathematical statement.
glossary.example_text: The sum s=x₁+x₂ does not determine x₁ on all of R². On the restricted inputs (t,t), it does: x₁=s/2.

glossary.definition: Recovery of a requested answer F(x) by a rule G using only a summary R(x), with F=G∘R on the declared input set. Such a rule on the attained summaries exists exactly when F has the same value on every fiber of R.
glossary.example_text: From R(x₁,x₂)=x₁+x₂, the answer H(x₁,x₂)=2x₁+2x₂ is recovered by G(s)=2s. The first coordinate alone is not recoverable on all real pairs.
glossary.note: The fiber criterion establishes existence. Continuity, stability, and efficient evaluation require their own hypotheses.

glossary.definition: Two admissible inputs u,v with R(u)=R(v) but F(u)≠F(v). They prove that no function of the summary R alone recovers the requested answer F on the whole declared input set.
glossary.example_text: The inputs (1,0) and (0,1) have the same sum 1 but different first coordinates. For linear R and F, their difference w=(1,−1) gives Rw=0 and Fw=1.

glossary.definition: The span of a matrix’s row vectors over its declared coefficient field. When rows represent scalar measurements, their row space is the set of all linear combinations of those measurements.
glossary.example_text: The rows (1,1,0) and (0,1,1) span the target row (1,2,1), obtained by adding them. Thus adding the corresponding two measurements recovers that target exactly.
glossary.quick_example: The rows (1,1) and (2,2) span the one-dimensional row space of [[1,1],[2,2]].

glossary.definition: For a projector P and a linear operator T, the map (I−P)TP records output leaving the retained range after the input starts in that range. It vanishes exactly when that range is invariant under T.
glossary.example_text: With P=diag(1,0), T=[[1,2],[3,4]], and x=(2,0)ᵀ, the full output is (2,6)ᵀ and the retained output is (2,0)ᵀ. The leakage is (0,6)ᵀ.
glossary.note: For an arbitrary input, T−PTP also includes transfers starting in the discarded input range. The single leakage term is not the whole residual in that setting.

glossary.definition: Given representation maps R_X,R_Y, an operation f, and a proposed transferred rule f̄, the discrepancy Δ_f(x)=R_Y(f(x))−f̄(R_X(x)). The subtraction requires a common vector-space output. The defect depends on the proposed rule and the input.
glossary.example_text: For f(x₁,x₂)=x₁x₂, R_X(x)=x₁+x₂, R_Y=I, and f̄(s)=s²/4, the defect at (2,3) is 6−25/4=−1/4. The candidate is exact on inputs (t,t).
glossary.note: A pointwise defect can be nonlinear. Failure of one proposed rule is not by itself an obstruction to every possible rule.

glossary.definition: A spanning family in a finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product space, used to analyze a vector through its inner products with the family. A frame may contain redundant vectors. In orthonormal coordinates, its analysis matrix A has full column rank and admits a left inverse.
glossary.example_text: The vectors (1,0), (0,1) and (1,1) give A(a,b) = (a,b,a+b). Three measurements recover a vector in R², although the three frame vectors are not a basis.

glossary.definition: Positive constants α and β such that α‖x‖² ≤ ‖Ax‖² ≤ β‖x‖² for every input x of a frame analysis map A. The lower bound ensures that analysis loses no vector direction. Both bounds depend on the declared inner products and normalization.
glossary.example_text: For A(a,b) = (a,b,a+b), ‖Ax‖² = a²+b²+(a+b)² lies between ‖x‖² and 3‖x‖² in Euclidean norm. The optimal bounds are α = 1 and β = 3.

glossary.definition: For a finite frame analysis map A with fixed inner products, the operator G = A* A on the original vector space. In orthonormal stored coordinates, * is conjugate transpose. G is positive definite and invertible when A has full column rank. Its inverse gives canonical dual synthesis G⁻¹A*.
glossary.example_text: The example's analysis matrix gives G = [[2,1],[1,2]], with eigenvalues 1 and 3. This is different from the reconstruction SA = I₂ and the coefficient projection AS.

glossary.definition: For a finite full-column-rank analysis matrix A in orthonormal coordinates, the synthesis S = (A* A)⁻¹A*. It satisfies SA = I, while AS is the orthogonal projector onto the image of A. For fixed A, applying S is linear. Constructing S as A varies requires the rank condition.
glossary.example_text: For A(a,b) = (a,b,a+b), canonical dual synthesis is S = (1/3)[[2,−1,1],[−1,2,1]]. It sends (2,3,5) back to (2,3).

glossary.definition: For a real or complex matrix A in Euclidean coordinates, the unique matrix A⁺ satisfying AA⁺A = A, A⁺AA⁺ = A⁺, (AA⁺)* = AA⁺ and (A⁺A)* = A⁺A. It is defined even for rectangular or rank-deficient matrices. AA⁺ and A⁺A are orthogonal projectors on the respective coordinate spaces.
glossary.example_text: For the full-column-rank matrix A in Example 6, A⁺ is the displayed synthesis S. Thus A⁺A = I₂ but AA⁺ ≠ I₃.
glossary.note: A pseudoinverse does not recover directions in the kernel of A. With nonorthonormal coordinates, metric choices must be carried explicitly.
glossary.quick_example: For the column A = (1,1)ᵀ, A† = (1/2,1/2). Thus A†A = 1, while AA† projects onto equal-coordinate pairs.

glossary.definition: For linear analysis A and linear synthesis S satisfying SA = I, the map P = AS on coefficient space. It satisfies P² = P, has image im A and kernel ker S, and sends any coefficient vector to analyzed coordinates representing the same underlying vector. It need not be orthogonal for an arbitrary left inverse S.
glossary.example_text: The triple c = (0,0,1) is not in im A. Its projection is AS c = (1/3,1/3,2/3), whose third coordinate is the sum of the first two.

glossary.definition: For linear maps A and S with SA = I and a coefficient selector Eᵢ, the map Cᵢ = SEᵢA on the original space. When the selectors partition all coordinates, the Cᵢ sum to the identity. In a redundant system, an individual Cᵢ need not be idempotent, so additive reconstruction alone does not make it a projector.
glossary.example_text: The first component is C₁ = (1/3)[[2,0],[−1,0]]. It satisfies C₁² = (2/3)C₁ ≠ C₁, even though C₁+C₂+C₃ = I₂.

glossary.definition: The kernel of a linear synthesis map S in a redundant linear presentation. Adding g ∈ ker S to a coefficient vector c leaves the represented vector unchanged because S(c+g) = Sc. The quotient of coefficient space by ker S records the represented vectors. For SA = I, (I−AS)c is the gauge part of c.
glossary.example_text: For the displayed synthesis S, the nonzero vector g = (−1,−1,1) satisfies Sg = 0. Coefficients c and c+g therefore synthesize to the same vector.

glossary.definition: In a finite linear presentation with Euclidean inner products on the stored spaces, H = S* S pulls the underlying vector geometry back to coefficient space: c*Hd = (Sc)*(Sd). H is positive semidefinite and its kernel is ker S. It gives a genuine inner product after quotienting out those gauge directions.
glossary.example_text: With the example's synthesis S and g = (−1,−1,1), g*Hg = ‖Sg‖² = 0 although g is nonzero. This coefficient metric is singular.
glossary.note: For an underlying metric Q rather than the identity, the pulled-back coefficient metric is S*QS.

glossary.definition: The adjoint of a linear map T:X→Y for declared positive-definite Hermitian metric matrices Q_X and Q_Y. In stored coordinates it is T♯ = Q_X⁻¹T*Q_Y, where * is raw conjugate transpose. It satisfies ⟨Tx,y⟩_Y = ⟨x,T♯y⟩_X. The formula requires Q_X to be invertible.
glossary.example_text: Using the example's analysis A with source metric Q_X = A*A and target metric Q_Y = I₃ makes A♯ = (A*A)⁻¹A*, the displayed canonical synthesis S.
glossary.note: A singular coefficient metric cannot be inverted by this formula. Its gauge directions require a quotient or a separately justified generalized inverse.

glossary.definition: A linear functional from a vector space to its coefficient field. With column-vector coordinates, it is stored as a row ℓ and acts by ℓx. Covectors form the dual space. A chosen inner product can identify vectors with covectors, but that identification depends on the metric.
glossary.example_text: The sum observation R(a,b) = a+b is the covector (1,1). The requested first-coordinate observation F(a,b) = a is the covector (1,0).

glossary.definition: For a linear map A:X→Y and a covector ℓ on Y, the covector ℓA on X, defined by (ℓA)(x) = ℓ(Ax). Pullback composes an observation with the map and does not require A to be invertible. Under a coordinate change y = Cx, storing the same observation in y coordinates instead gives the row ℓC⁻¹.
glossary.example_text: Pulling the scalar observation ℓ(s) = 2s back along R(a,b) = a+b gives ℓR(a,b) = 2a+2b. Its row is (2,2).

glossary.definition: A real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrix Q for which x*Qx > 0 for every nonzero vector x. It defines an inner product and is invertible. Positive semidefiniteness only requires x*Qx ≥ 0 and can allow nonzero vectors of zero length.
glossary.example_text: For the example's analysis matrix, Q = A*A = [[2,1],[1,2]]. Its quadratic form is a²+b²+(a+b)², which is positive whenever (a,b) ≠ (0,0).
glossary.quick_example: diag(1,3) is positive definite because x²+3y² > 0 for every nonzero pair.

glossary.definition: A nonnegative function satisfying absolute homogeneity and the triangle inequality, while allowing a nonzero vector to have value zero. For linear synthesis S from a redundant coefficient space, p(c) = ‖Sc‖ is a seminorm whose zero directions are exactly ker S. Passing to the quotient by those directions gives a norm.
glossary.example_text: The coefficient vector g = (−1,−1,1) is nonzero but satisfies ‖Sg‖ = 0 for the example's synthesis map. Its ordinary Euclidean norm is √3.
glossary.quick_example: p(x,y) = |x| is a seminorm on R² that vanishes on every vertical vector.

glossary.definition: The formal series A(z) = Σₙ≥₀ aₙzⁿ used to store a sequence (aₙ). The coefficient of zⁿ is aₙ itself. This convention determines the multiplication rule and differs from factorial normalization.
glossary.example_text: The reciprocal of 1+z+z² is (1−z)/(1−z³), with ordinary coefficient pattern 1, −1, 0, 1, −1, 0, ….
glossary.note: Formal coefficient identities do not by themselves justify evaluating the series outside its convergence region.

glossary.definition: The formal series A(t) = Σₙ≥₀ aₙtⁿ/n! over a coefficient field of characteristic zero. The sequence entry aₙ is the coefficient in the basis tⁿ/n!, while the ordinary coefficient of tⁿ is aₙ/n!.
glossary.example_text: The Bell numbers have EGF exp(eᵗ−1). Its degree-five term is 52t⁵/5!, because B₅ = 52.
glossary.note: The Euler demonstration uses the compressed index n for degree 2n. Its secant denominator is (2n)!, not n!.

glossary.definition: The product rule for exponentially normalized series: if A(t) = Σ aₙtⁿ/n! and B(t) = Σ bₙtⁿ/n!, their product has coefficient cₙ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ binom(n,k)aₖbₙ₋ₖ in that same basis.
glossary.example_text: In the secant recurrence, the degree-four row is s₂ = 6s₁ − s₀ = 5. The factor 6 is binom(4,2).

glossary.term: Stirling numbers of the second kind
glossary.definition: The integers S(n,k) counting partitions of an n-element labelled set into k nonempty, unlabelled blocks. For n ≥ 1 they satisfy S(n,k) = S(n−1,k−1) + kS(n−1,k), with S(0,0) = 1 and zero outside 0 ≤ k ≤ n.
glossary.example_text: The row at n = 5 is (0,1,15,25,10,1). In particular, S(5,3) = 7+3·6 = 25.
glossary.quick_example: S(3,2) = 3: the singleton can be any of the three labels, with the other two in the second block.

glossary.term: Signed Stirling numbers of the first kind
glossary.definition: The coefficients s(n,k) in x(x−1)⋯(x−n+1) = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ s(n,k)xᵏ. Their lower-triangular matrix is the inverse of the second-kind Stirling matrix. The sign is part of this convention.
glossary.example_text: The n = 5 coefficient row is (0,24,−50,35,−10,1). Applied to (F₀,…,F₅), it gives 24−150+455−750+541 = 120 = 5!.
glossary.note: Unsigned first-kind Stirling numbers count permutations by cycles and remove these alternating signs. They are not the inverse matrix used here.

glossary.definition: The triangular sequence map cₙ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ S(n,k)aₖ. Each output uses finitely many input entries. Signed first-kind Stirling numbers invert the full triangular map, and the EGF form is C(t) = A(eᵗ−1).
glossary.example_text: Weights aₖ = 1 produce Bell numbers. Weights aₖ = k! produce Fubini numbers through the same matrix.
glossary.note: Recovering an input sequence from all preceding output values is different from recovering an arbitrary partition row from a single row sum.

glossary.definition: The integers Bₙ counting all partitions of an n-element labelled set into nonempty, unlabelled blocks. Equivalently Bₙ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ S(n,k), with B₀ = 1.
glossary.example_text: Adding the n = 5 Stirling row gives B₅ = 1+15+25+10+1 = 52.

glossary.definition: The integers Fₙ counting partitions of an n-element labelled set whose blocks are linearly ordered. A partition with k blocks has k! possible block orders, so Fₙ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ k!S(n,k), with F₀ = 1.
The polynomial Tₙ(z) = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ S(n,k)zᵏ retaining the complete partition row as coefficients. Evaluation at z = 1 gives Bₙ. Applying the functional zᵏ ↦ k! gives Fₙ.
glossary.example_text: T₅(z) = z+15z²+25z³+10z⁴+z⁵. Its value at 1 is 52, while ∫₀∞ e⁻ᵘT₅(u) du = 541.
glossary.note: The one-variable Touchard family is distinct from the multivariable partial Bell polynomials, which encode a different set of inputs.
glossary.quick_example: T₃(z) = z+3z²+z³. Its value at 1 is B₃ = 5.

glossary.definition: For m ≥ 2 and 0 ≤ r < m, work over a field containing a primitive mth root ζ and in which m is invertible. The operator Pᵣf(z) = (1/m)Σₗ₌₀ᵐ⁻¹ ζ⁻ʳˡf(ζˡz) selects precisely the monomials whose degrees are congruent to r modulo m. The polynomial identity also applies coefficientwise to formal series.
glossary.example_text: On a monomial zᵏ, the multiplier (1/m)Σₗ ζˡ⁽ᵏ⁻ʳ⁾ equals one when k ≡ r modulo m and zero otherwise.
glossary.note: The coefficient selector itself does not require roots of unity. This averaging formula needs both the stated root and division by m. A different polynomial basis requires transporting the projector through its basis change.

glossary.definition: For integers N ≥ 1 and n ≥ 0, a product of n factors in one arithmetic progression: (a)ₙ;N = ∏ₖ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹(a+Nk), with empty product one. Splitting the factors of a factorial into disjoint residue lanes gives an exact product decomposition.
glossary.example_text: The lane starting at 5 with step 10 and three factors is 5·15·25 = 1875. Taking three factors in each of the ten lanes starting at 5 through 14, multiplying the lanes, then multiplying by 4!, reconstructs 34!.
glossary.note: A multiplicative lane of factors and an additive residue section of a series are different objects. The factorial demonstration explicitly relates them.

glossary.definition: The coefficient-defined series ₚF_q(a₁,…,aₚ; b₁,…,b_q; z) = Σₙ≥₀ [(a₁)ₙ⋯(aₚ)ₙ/((b₁)ₙ⋯(b_q)ₙ)]zⁿ/n!, where (a)ₙ = a(a+1)⋯(a+n−1). The denominator factors must be defined and nonzero for the terms being used.
glossary.example_text: The identity (r)ₙ;10 = 10ⁿ(r/10)ₙ converts the selected exponential section into a ₀F₉ series. The parameter r/10 = 1 supplies the separate n! factor.
glossary.note: The displayed identity is coefficientwise. Analytic convergence depends on the parameters and the argument. Terminating cases also require the appropriate denominator conditions.

glossary.definition: In the Euler demonstration, the sequence Eⱼ is defined by sech(t) = Σⱼ≥₀ Eⱼtʲ/j!. Odd entries vanish and even entries alternate in sign. The sign and index convention must be fixed before comparing Euler tables.
aliases: Euler numbers in the sech convention
glossary.example_text: E₀ = 1, E₂ = −1, E₄ = 5 and E₆ = −61. The sequence a(n) = E₂ₙ has a(1) = −1, although E₁ = 0.

glossary.definition: The positive coefficients sₙ defined by sec(t) = Σₙ≥₀ sₙt²ⁿ/(2n)!. Their compressed index n refers to ordinary degree 2n. In the signed sech convention, E₂ₙ = (−1)ⁿsₙ.
glossary.example_text: The first values are 1, 1, 5, 61, 1385, 50521 and 2702765. Thus s₆ = 2702765 is the coefficient of t¹²/12!, not t⁶/6!.

glossary.definition: Substitution A(u(t)) of one formal series into another. If u has zero constant term, each output coefficient receives only finitely many contributions, so an arbitrary formal A can be composed without an analytic convergence assumption.
glossary.example_text: Substituting u(t) = eᵗ−1 into the weight EGF A(u) gives the transformed EGF C(t) = A(eᵗ−1).
glossary.note: If A is a polynomial, substitution is also a finite operation without the zero-constant-term condition. General infinite outer series need a valid formal or analytic setting.

glossary.term: Compositional inverse of a formal series
glossary.definition: For a formal series u(t) over a field with u(0) = 0 and nonzero linear coefficient, the unique series v(t) with v(0) = 0 satisfying u(v(t)) = t and v(u(t)) = t. The inverse concerns substitution.
glossary.example_text: The compositional inverse of eᵗ−1 is log(1+t). Consequently C(t) = A(eᵗ−1) is inverted by A(u) = C(log(1+u)).
glossary.note: A formal reciprocal solves u(t)v(t) = 1 and requires a nonzero constant coefficient. These are different inverse operations with different hypotheses.
glossary.quick_example: The substitution inverse of u(t) = 2t is v(t) = t/2. Their product is not the identity being tested.

glossary.definition: For a prime p and a nonzero rational x, vₚ(x) is the exponent of p in its reduced numerator minus the exponent in its reduced denominator. Set vₚ(0) = ∞. A rational is p-adically integral when its valuation is nonnegative.
glossary.example_text: The factorial-lane recurrence gives C₂ = 178205/966966. Its numerator contains one factor of 5 and its denominator contains none, so v₅(C₂) = 1.

glossary.definition: An invertible element of the p-adic integers. For a rational number, being a p-adic unit means vₚ(x) = 0: its reduced numerator and denominator are both coprime to p.
glossary.example_text: g₁ = 1/1001 is a 5-adic unit and can be reduced modulo powers of 5. C₂ = 178205/966966 is 5-adically integral but is not a unit.
glossary.note: A p-adically integral rational number need not be an ordinary integer, and a p-adically integral number of positive valuation is not a unit.
glossary.quick_example: The rational 3/5 is a 2-adic unit because both numerator and denominator are odd.

glossary.definition: A linear filter given by finitely many taps, or coefficients, applied to specified shifts of a signal. In a causal convention yₙ = Σₗ₌₀ᴸ⁻¹ hₗxₙ₋ₗ. A finite signal also needs a boundary rule, such as zero extension or circular indexing.
glossary.example_text: On the sixteen-sample circular signal, H = I+2T−T² gives (Hx)₁₀ = 12+2(−4)−(−4) = 8.
glossary.note: The worked wavelet example uses circular indexing. The catalog’s causal FIR entry uses zero extension. The transfer formula must retain the chosen boundary convention.

glossary.definition: The extra shift in a phase coordinate required when an index crosses a residue boundary. Splitting a signal into residue phases changes both the phase label and, when necessary, the position within that phase.
glossary.example_text: For even and odd rows E and O, one backward circular shift sends the even output to ZO and the odd output to E. Its two-phase matrix is [[0,Z],[I,0]], with Z the half-rate delay.
glossary.note: Forward shifts place the carry in a different block from backward shifts. Its position follows from the index convention.

glossary.definition: For a complex vector x of length N ≥ 1, the convention used here is x̂ₖ = Σₙ₌₀ᴺ⁻¹ xₙ exp(−2πikn/N). The inverse uses the positive exponential sign and divides by N.
glossary.note: A different normalization may distribute the factor 1/N between the two maps. Changing conventions changes their matrix entries.

glossary.definition: A coordinate transform of a real vector of length N ≥ 1 using cosine samples. The catalog fixes orthonormal DCT-II: yₖ = αₖΣₙ₌₀ᴺ⁻¹xₙ cos(π(n+1/2)k/N), where α₀ = 1/√N and αₖ = √(2/N) for k > 0.
glossary.note: DCT type and normalization are part of the definition. The COS probability method uses a Fourier-cosine expansion but is not simply this finite data transform.

glossary.definition: For a real matrix A, either K = AAᵀ on its output space or H = AᵀA on its input space. Both are positive semidefinite. Their positive eigenvalues agree with multiplicity, although their dimensions and zero-eigenvalue multiplicities can differ.
glossary.note: For a column partition A = [A₁ … A_B], the exact identity AAᵀ = Σ_b A_bA_bᵀ retains every column. Dropping a block changes the operator.

glossary.definition: A representation of a real factor A in coordinates on a chosen subspace. If Q has orthonormal columns and the range of A is contained in the range of Q, then B = QᵀA gives A = QB. The matrices BBᵀ and AAᵀ have the same nonzero spectrum, including multiplicity. The core is smaller when Q has fewer columns than A has rows.
glossary.note: If the chosen subspace misses part of the range, the omitted residual requires a separate bound. A floating-point rank threshold does not establish exact range capture.

glossary.definition: For a real random variable Q, φ(t) = E[exp(itQ)] at real frequency t. It encodes the probability law in Fourier coordinates. Unlike a real moment-generating function, it is defined for every real t because the integrand has modulus one.
glossary.note: For an admissible exponential tilt with cumulant generator κ, the monograph uses φθ(t) = exp(κ(θ+it)−κ(θ)). The domain and logarithm branch are stated with that transform.

glossary.definition: A random variable Q = XᵀMX with real Gaussian vector X and symmetric matrix M. In the central positive case X has mean zero and covariance Σ, M is positive semidefinite, and Q has the same law as ΣⱼλⱼZⱼ² for independent standard normal Zⱼ and eigenvalues λⱼ of Σ¹ᐟ²MΣ¹ᐟ².
aliases: Quadratic form of a Gaussian vector
glossary.note: The zero-mean assumption gives the central reduction. Positive semidefiniteness makes the eigenvalues nonnegative and the law supported on [0,∞), as required by the positive-tail formula. A central indefinite form has the same reduction with signed eigenvalues. Noncentral forms require their additional parameters. With no nonzero eigenvalues, Q is identically zero.

glossary.definition: A Fourier-cosine method for evaluating distributional quantities from characteristic-function values. K-COS applies this representation to Gaussian quadratic-form tails, with a stated window, retained mode count, spectral approximation and error bounds.
glossary.note: The positive-tail formula uses frequencies kπ/b on [0,b] and half weight on the zero mode. A finite sum is an approximation until the applicable remainders and numerical arithmetic have been controlled.

glossary.definition: In K-COS, a nonempty group P of eigenvalues represented by its count n, mean μ and centered power sums Mₘ = Σⱼ∈P(λⱼ−μ)ᵐ. Thus M₀ = n and M₁ = 0. Truncated transform expansions also carry a remainder bound.
glossary.note: The expansion needs |2s/(1−2sμ)|·maxⱼ|λⱼ−μ| < 1 on the frequencies and tilt being used. Nearby eigenvalues alone do not establish that condition for every query.

glossary.definition: An interval guaranteed to contain the specified exact quantity. Its finite arithmetic rounds outward, and its final endpoints include every required analytic remainder. The claim concerns the encoded inputs and stated mathematical model.
glossary.note: For a probability interval [p₋,p₊], the stated relative acceptance test requires p₋ > 0 and p₊/p₋−1 ≤ ε. A narrow interval is insufficient if a required source of error was omitted.
