glossary.definition: A sum of justified bounds for the approximation steps in a mathematical model. The K-COS budget separates spectral-packet approximation, support and cosine-folding error, and omitted Fourier modes.
glossary.note: These real or complex arithmetic bounds do not automatically enclose floating-point rounding. A numerical certificate must also account for its finite arithmetic and exact-input interpretation.

glossary.definition: For a vector space V over a field, the vector space V* of linear scalar-valued functions on V. Its elements are covectors or linear functionals. In finite coordinates a row vector acts on a column vector, but identifying covectors with vectors requires additional choices.
glossary.quick_example: On pairs, ℓ(x,y) = 2x−y is a covector. It sends (3,4) to 2.

glossary.definition: For a subspace W of an inner-product space, W⊥ consists of all vectors perpendicular to every vector in W. In finite dimensions the space decomposes as the orthogonal direct sum W ⊕ W⊥.
glossary.quick_example: In Euclidean R², the perpendicular complement of span{(1,1)} is span{(1,−1)}.
glossary.note: Perpendicularity depends on the inner product. A weighted inner product can change the complement.

glossary.definition: A basis whose vectors have norm one and are pairwise perpendicular in the chosen inner product. In finite real or complex coordinates, the matrix Q with these basis columns satisfies Q*Q = I.
glossary.quick_example: The Haar vectors (1,1)/√2 and (1,−1)/√2 form an orthonormal basis of Euclidean R².

glossary.definition: A nonnegative square root of an eigenvalue of A*A for a real or complex matrix A, with zero-padding conventions stated when needed. The largest singular value is the induced Euclidean operator norm. Singular values describe gain and rank without requiring A to be square.
glossary.quick_example: For A = [[0,2],[3,0]], A*A = diag(9,4), so its singular values are 3 and 2.
glossary.note: A small computed singular value needs a tolerance or enclosure before it is treated as exactly zero.

glossary.definition: A factorization A = UΣV* of a finite real or complex matrix, where U and V are orthogonal or unitary and Σ is rectangular diagonal with nonnegative entries. These entries are the singular values. It separates input directions, gains and output directions.
glossary.quick_example: The diagonal matrix diag(3,1) already has an SVD with U = V = I and Σ = diag(3,1).
glossary.note: Truncating an SVD changes the operator unless all omitted singular values are zero.

glossary.definition: A complex square matrix T satisfying T*T = TT*. In finite complex dimensions, normal matrices admit an orthonormal eigenbasis. Hermitian and unitary matrices are normal; an arbitrary diagonalizable matrix need not be normal.
glossary.quick_example: The nonzero nilpotent matrix [[0,1],[0,0]] is not normal: T*T = diag(0,1), while TT* = diag(1,0).

glossary.definition: For a finite real or complex matrix A, the norm defined by ‖A‖HS² = tr(A*A), equal to the sum of the squared absolute values of its entries. It measures matrix size in the specified orthonormal coordinates and differs from the largest-singular-value operator norm.
glossary.quick_example: For diag(3,4), the Hilbert–Schmidt norm is 5, while the induced Euclidean norm is 4.

glossary.definition: An operation U whose square is the identity: U² = I. Applying it twice restores the input. A linear involution over a field where 2 is invertible splits the space into its +1 and −1 eigenspaces via (I+U)/2 and (I−U)/2.
glossary.quick_example: Reflection of a polynomial, Uf(x) = f(−x), is an involution. Its +1 and −1 parts are the even and odd polynomials.
glossary.note: The identity U² = I does not by itself make U orthogonal or unitary.

glossary.definition: The set of outputs obtained from one input by the declared allowed operations. For a single operator T, its forward orbit is {v,Tv,T²v,…}. Taking the linear span of an orbit is a further step in the definition of a cyclic vector.
glossary.quick_example: If T swaps two coordinates, the orbit of (1,0) is {(1,0),(0,1)}; its span is all of R².

glossary.definition: A retained description of an operation. For a projector P and operator T, PTP acts on the retained range. For a summary R and a chosen lift S, RTS is a candidate reduced operation. Exact agreement with all original inputs requires an additional compatibility condition.
glossary.quick_example: For T = [[1,2],[3,4]] and P = diag(1,0), PTP retains only the upper-left entry 1.
glossary.note: A compression can be useful even when the retained state does not determine its own exact future.

glossary.definition: A linear map preserving the specified norm of every input. Between finite inner-product spaces, preserving inner products is equivalent. In orthonormal coordinates an isometric embedding Q satisfies Q*Q = I; it need not be onto its codomain.
glossary.quick_example: The map x ↦ (x,0) preserves Euclidean length. Its matrix is rectangular, so it is not a unitary automorphism of R².

glossary.definition: A scalar-valued function B(u,v) linear separately in u and v. Over the real numbers a matrix M gives B(u,v) = uᵀMv. Symmetry, positivity and nondegeneracy are additional properties rather than part of bilinearity.
glossary.quick_example: B(u,v) = u₁v₁−u₂v₂ is symmetric and bilinear, but B((0,1),(0,1)) = −1, so it is not an inner product.
glossary.note: For complex inner products one argument is conjugate-linear. That pairing is sesquilinear.

glossary.definition: In the real finite-dimensional setting, a scalar expression q(x) = xᵀMx, usually written with M symmetric. In complex Hermitian geometry the corresponding real-valued expression is x*Mx with M Hermitian. Positivity asks whether this value is nonnegative for every input.
glossary.quick_example: With M = [[1,1],[1,1]], q(x,y) = (x+y)². It is nonnegative and vanishes on the nonzero direction (1,−1).

glossary.definition: A family of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is the whole set. Each element lies in exactly one block. A finer partition divides coarse blocks into smaller blocks; this set-theoretic use of block is distinct from an operator matrix block.
glossary.quick_example: The partition {{0,2},{1,3}} groups four indices by parity. The singleton partition refines it.

glossary.term: Sufficient summary for a requested output
glossary.definition: A map R that retains enough information to determine a specified output F: there is a map G on the attained summary values such that F = G∘R. Equivalently, F is constant on each fiber of R. Sufficiency is relative to the requested output and admissible inputs.
glossary.quick_example: R(x,y) = x+y is sufficient for F(x,y) = 2(x+y), but is insufficient for recovering x on all of R².
glossary.note: This deterministic recovery definition is separate from statistical sufficiency for a family of probability laws.

glossary.definition: For a vector space V and subspace K, the canonical linear map V → V/K sending x to its equivalence class x+K. Its kernel is K and it is surjective. It retains exactly the distinction between inputs differing by an element of K.
glossary.quick_example: Quotienting R² by span{(1,−1)} identifies all pairs with the same sum.

glossary.definition: The size of an approximation error measured in a stated norm, such as |x−x̂| for scalars or ‖x−x̂‖ for vectors. It retains the units and scale of the quantity. An acceptance threshold must use the same units and norm.
glossary.quick_example: Approximating 100 by 99 gives absolute error 1, while approximating 0.001 by 0 gives absolute error 0.001.

glossary.definition: An absolute error divided by a specified nonzero reference size. With exact target x, a common rule is ‖x−x̂‖/‖x‖ when x ≠ 0. The reference and zero-target rule must be stated.
glossary.quick_example: Approximating 100 by 99 gives relative error 1/100. Approximating 0.001 by 0 gives relative error 1.
glossary.note: A small absolute error can have a large relative error near zero.

glossary.definition: The difference between a computed output and the exact output of the declared problem on the declared input. A forward bound controls the answer directly. It can include effects from input uncertainty, operator approximation and finite arithmetic.
glossary.quick_example: For the equation 2x = 6, a computed answer x̂ = 2.9 has absolute forward error 0.1.

glossary.definition: The size of an allowed perturbation to the input data that makes the computed answer an exact solution. The data components allowed to change and their norm determine the backward-error problem. Small backward error gives a useful forward guarantee only with suitable conditioning.
glossary.quick_example: For 2x = 6, x̂ = 2.9 exactly solves 2x = 5.8. If only the right side may change, that perturbation has absolute size 0.2.

glossary.definition: Arithmetic on sets represented by intervals, with operations producing intervals that contain all allowed exact outputs. Finite implementations need outward rounding. Repeated occurrences of an uncertain quantity can widen an enclosure because interval endpoints do not record all dependencies.
glossary.quick_example: For x in [1,2], direct interval subtraction gives x−x in [−1,1], although the expression is identically zero when both occurrences denote the same x.

glossary.definition: A linear map T between normed spaces for which a finite constant C satisfies ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖x‖ for every input. Its induced norm is the least such bound. All linear maps between finite-dimensional normed spaces are bounded; infinite-dimensional cases need this hypothesis.
glossary.quick_example: Multiplication of every coordinate by 2 on Euclidean space is bounded with induced norm 2.

glossary.definition: A recorded sequence of inference steps showing how admitted leaves and previously established conclusions reach a target. Each step must cite an allowed rule with all its premises available. Checking a trace establishes its validity within the declared rule system.
glossary.quick_example: Admit s₁ and s₃, derive a,b,c,d using their recorded rules, then apply {a,b,c,d} ⇒ t.
glossary.note: A valid trace in a supplied proof field does not establish the soundness of arbitrary externally supplied rules.

glossary.definition: An established node used by more than one later inference. Sharing allows a derivation to be represented as a directed acyclic graph instead of copying the whole premise derivation into each branch. Costs depend on whether reused nodes are charged once or once per use.
glossary.quick_example: In the certificate example, s₁ supplies both a and b but its selected-leaf cost is charged only once.

glossary.definition: An admissible instance on which a claimed universal conclusion fails. A counterexample must satisfy the claim’s hypotheses. For a recovery claim, two admissible inputs with the same summary and different requested outputs provide a collision counterexample.
glossary.quick_example: The pairs (1,0) and (0,1) have the same sum and different first coordinates, disproving recovery of the first coordinate from the sum alone.

glossary.definition: A condition that must hold whenever a requested property holds. If A implies B, then B is necessary for A. Failing B rules out A, but passing B alone need not establish A.
glossary.quick_example: Equal reflection magnitude is necessary for cyclic reachability on the Smith chart. A prescribed finite rotation order also restricts the phase.

glossary.definition: A condition that guarantees the requested property. If A implies B, then A is sufficient for B. The same implication makes B necessary for A. An equivalence provides both directions.
glossary.quick_example: For linear F and R on a common vector space, ker R contained in ker F is sufficient for recovering F from R on the whole space.

glossary.definition: A search that has established neither a valid witness nor a proof that none exists within the specified problem. A timeout, an exhausted budget or rejection of one proposed certificate can leave the existence question unresolved.
glossary.quick_example: Rejecting the one-leaf proposal {s₁} leaves the valid two-leaf certificate {s₁,s₃} available.

glossary.definition: A proposition expressed in a proof assistant’s language with explicit types, hypotheses and conclusion. Its relationship to a written theorem depends on the interpretation of every object and assumption. A declaration name alone does not specify that relationship.
glossary.quick_example: A declaration proving a finite matrix identity covers that identity under its encoded hypotheses; it does not automatically cover an infinite-dimensional analogue.

glossary.definition: A computation with enough recorded inputs, source identity, environment information and instructions to repeat the stated check. Reproduction should compare the promised outputs or invariants. Repeating a calculation preserves the scope of the calculation rather than extending it.
glossary.quick_example: A source archive, its hash, the arithmetic convention and the expected rational output let another reader replay one exact example.

glossary.definition: For a nonzero polynomial, the largest exponent having a nonzero coefficient. Over a field, degrees add under multiplication of nonzero polynomials. The zero polynomial needs a separate convention, often degree −∞, when degree formulas include it.
glossary.quick_example: The polynomial 4−2x+3x³ has degree 3. A falling-factorial basis element b₃ also has ordinary degree 3.

glossary.definition: A nonzero polynomial whose highest-degree coefficient is one. A sequence with one monic polynomial of each degree gives an invertible triangular change from ordinary powers on every finite degree range.
glossary.quick_example: x(x−1)(x−2) = x³−3x²+2x is monic. The constant polynomial 1 is monic of degree zero.

glossary.definition: A square matrix with every entry on one side of its diagonal zero. A unitriangular matrix also has all diagonal entries equal to one, so it is invertible over any field. Triangular coordinate maps let successive coefficients be recovered in order.
glossary.quick_example: The lower-triangular matrix [[1,0],[3,1]] sends (a,b) to (a,3a+b); recover b by subtracting 3a.

glossary.definition: The least positive integer p for which adding the multiplicative identity to itself p times gives zero, if such an integer exists; otherwise the characteristic is zero. Positive field characteristic is always prime. Division by integers in formulas must respect this value.
glossary.quick_example: In the field with three elements, 1+1+1 = 0. A formula dividing by 3 cannot be used there.
glossary.note: Falling-factorial coordinate maps remain monic triangular in positive characteristic, but derivative and roots-of-unity arguments can require additional hypotheses.

glossary.definition: The finite product (a)ₙ = a(a+1)⋯(a+n−1), with (a)₀ = 1. This is the Pochhammer convention used in the hypergeometric series entry. The notation must be distinguished from falling factorials and from the step-N factorial lanes.
glossary.quick_example: (2)₃ = 2·3·4 = 24, while the falling factorial 2(2−1)(2−2) is zero.

glossary.definition: The coefficient rule for multiplying ordinary formal power series: the coefficient of zⁿ in A(z)B(z) is Σₖ₌₀ⁿ aₖbₙ₋ₖ. Each coefficient uses finitely many terms, so this formal rule needs no analytic convergence assumption.
glossary.quick_example: The coefficient of z² in (1+2z+3z²)(1+4z+5z²) is 5+8+3 = 16.

glossary.definition: An infinite coefficient list written as Σₙ≥₀ aₙzⁿ and manipulated coefficientwise over a declared ring. Addition and multiplication are algebraic operations on these lists. Evaluating the series at a numerical z is a separate analytic question.
glossary.quick_example: The identity (1−z)(1+z+z²+⋯) = 1 is valid formally even when no numerical value for z is chosen.

glossary.definition: For a complex power series centered at zero, the radius R such that the series converges absolutely for |z| < R and diverges for |z| > R. The endpoints R = 0 and R = ∞ are allowed. Boundary convergence must be checked separately.
glossary.quick_example: The geometric series Σₙ≥₀ zⁿ has radius 1. At z = 1 its terms do not tend to zero.

glossary.definition: For a function analytic near zero, the ordinary coefficient of zⁿ in its Taylor series is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)/n!. Its exponentially normalized coefficient is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0). The basis convention determines which number is called the stored coefficient.
glossary.quick_example: For exp(z), every derivative at zero is 1, while its ordinary coefficients are 1, 1, 1/2, 1/6, ….

glossary.definition: The polynomial operator ∇f(x) = f(x)−f(x−1), with unit step. It differs from the forward difference Δf(x) = f(x+1)−f(x). The falling-degree operator is x∇, while the falling-factorial lowering operator is Δ.
glossary.quick_example: For f(x) = x², ∇f = 2x−1 and Δf = 2x+1.

glossary.definition: A linear map between algebras that also preserves their specified multiplication; in the unital convention it preserves the identity element. A linear coordinate isomorphism alone need not satisfy the multiplication condition.
glossary.quick_example: The falling-factorial map sends z² to x(x−1), while the square of its value on z is x². It therefore fails to preserve ordinary multiplication.

glossary.definition: A shift of a finite length-N signal with indices reduced modulo N. Under the convention (Sx)ₙ = xₙ₋₁ mod N, the last sample moves to the first position. This boundary rule differs from zero extension.
glossary.quick_example: The circular delay sends (1,2,3,4) to (4,1,2,3).

glossary.definition: Retaining samples on a specified residue class: with factor m and phase r, yₖ = xₘₖ₊ᵣ. The phase and boundary convention are part of the operation. Retaining only one phase generally loses information about the others.
glossary.quick_example: Taking the even phase of (1,2,3,4) gives (1,3). Retaining the odd phase (2,4) as well permits interleaving back to the original signal.

glossary.definition: Failure of a sampling operation to distinguish different inputs. In frequency language, distinct oscillations can produce the same retained samples. Additional input restrictions or complementary filter-bank outputs are needed for exact recovery.
glossary.quick_example: On integer indices, the signals 1 and (−1)ⁿ both give the constant sequence 1 after retaining only even-indexed samples.

glossary.definition: A collection of filters and sampling maps sending one signal to several component streams. A synthesis bank combines those streams into an output signal. Perfect reconstruction is a property of the combined analysis and synthesis maps with their declared delays and boundary conventions.
glossary.quick_example: For a pair (u,v), the Haar analysis stores average (u+v)/2 and detail (u−v)/2; synthesis returns their sum and difference.

glossary.definition: An invertible update of one component using another, such as predicting odd samples from even samples and then updating the even stream with the prediction residual. The inverse undoes the updates in reverse order. This signal-processing meaning of lifting differs from lifting an object through a quotient.
glossary.quick_example: Set d = v−u, then a = u+d/2. Recover u = a−d/2 and v = u+d.

glossary.definition: An equality between the squared norm of an object and the correctly weighted squared magnitudes of its complete transform coefficients. Orthonormal coordinates use unit weights. Other normalizations change the weights, so energy formulas must follow the analysis convention.
glossary.quick_example: With a = (u+v)/2 and d = (u−v)/2, u²+v² = 2(a²+d²). The factor 2 belongs to this normalization.

glossary.definition: A rule supplying samples outside the stored finite signal, such as periodic continuation, zero extension or reflection. A filter’s taps do not determine its finite matrix until this rule and the indexing convention have been fixed.
glossary.quick_example: Delaying (1,2,3,4) by one sample gives (0,1,2,3) with zero extension and (4,1,2,3) with circular indexing.

glossary.definition: A quantum system with a two-dimensional complex state space. A pure state has a unit-vector representative α|0⟩+β|1⟩ with |α|²+|β|² = 1; multiplying both amplitudes by one global phase leaves the same density matrix. Mixed states use density matrices.
glossary.quick_example: The vector (3/5,4/5) is normalized because 9/25+16/25 = 1.

glossary.definition: A common unit-modulus factor multiplying every amplitude of a state vector. It cancels in |ψ⟩⟨ψ| and leaves the represented pure-state density matrix unchanged. This statement assumes the factor applies to the whole state being compared.
glossary.quick_example: The vectors (3/5,4/5) and (3i/5,4i/5) give the same density matrix.

glossary.definition: The phase difference between nonzero amplitudes in a chosen basis. It appears in off-diagonal density-matrix entries and can change interference probabilities even when the basis populations stay fixed.
glossary.quick_example: The states (3/5,4/5) and (3/5,−4/5) have the same Z probabilities but X-plus probabilities 49/50 and 1/50.

glossary.definition: A density matrix of the form ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ| for a unit vector ψ. In finite dimensions it has rank one, satisfies ρ² = ρ and has purity tr(ρ²) = 1. The vector representative is determined only up to global phase.

A density matrix that is not pure. In finite dimensions its purity is less than one, and it can be written as a convex mixture of pure-state density matrices. Such a decomposition is generally not unique.
glossary.quick_example: The dephased state diag(9/25,16/25) has purity 337/625, so it is mixed.

glossary.definition: A Hermitian operator E satisfying 0 ≤ E ≤ I. For density matrix ρ, tr(Eρ) is the probability of its associated outcome. Effects in a complete measurement sum to I. They need not individually be projectors.
glossary.quick_example: E = I/2 gives probability 1/2 for every state, although E² = I/4 differs from E.

glossary.definition: In the finite setting, a Hermitian operator whose real eigenvalues label possible outcomes of its projective measurement. Its expectation in state ρ is tr(Aρ). The operator and its measurement effects have related but different roles.
glossary.quick_example: The Pauli matrix Z = diag(1,−1) has mean 9/25−16/25 = −7/25 in the demonstration state.

glossary.definition: A linear completely positive, trace-preserving map on density matrices. A finite Kraus representation is Φ(ρ) = ΣⱼKⱼρKⱼ* with ΣⱼKⱼ*Kⱼ = I. Complete positivity requires positivity to survive extension by an arbitrary auxiliary quantum system.
glossary.quick_example: Coordinate dephasing uses K₀ = diag(1,0) and K₁ = diag(0,1), keeping the diagonal entries and deleting the off-diagonal entries.

glossary.definition: Reconstructing a state from probabilities for a sufficiently informative collection of measurement settings. For a qubit, exact X, Y and Z outcome probabilities determine its density matrix. Experimental estimates introduce sampling error and must still describe a positive state.
glossary.quick_example: For the phase-one demonstration state, X-plus = 49/50, Y-plus = 1/2 and Z-plus = 9/25 recover the upper-right entry 12/25.
glossary.note: One outcome from a single copy does not supply the three ensemble probabilities.

glossary.definition: A projective measurement with its outcome retained. Outcome j has probability pⱼ = tr(Pⱼρ); if pⱼ > 0, the conditional output state is PⱼρPⱼ/pⱼ. Discarding the outcome instead gives the sum ΣⱼPⱼρPⱼ.
glossary.quick_example: In the demonstration, retaining coordinate outcome zero gives the state |0⟩⟨0| with probability 9/25.
glossary.note: The conditional state formula is undefined for a zero-probability outcome.

glossary.definition: The complex voltage-to-current ratio of a linear one-port at a stated frequency, written Z = R+iX. Its real part is resistance and its imaginary part is reactance. The Smith-chart guide uses a positive real reference resistance Z₀ and normalized impedance z = Z/Z₀.
glossary.quick_example: The load Z = 25+i25 ohms with Z₀ = 50 ohms has normalized impedance z = (1+i)/2.

glossary.definition: The dimensionless ratio z = Z/Z₀ relative to a declared reference impedance. In the Smith-chart guide Z₀ is positive and real, so the real and imaginary parts are normalized resistance and reactance.
glossary.quick_example: Changing Z₀ from 50 to 25 ohms changes the coordinates of a 50-ohm resistor from z = 1 to z = 2, while the physical resistor stays the same.

glossary.definition: The reciprocal Y = 1/Z where Z is nonzero, measured in siemens. With normalized impedance z, normalized admittance is y = 1/z. Switching to the admittance grid changes the description of the same load.
glossary.quick_example: If z = (1+i)/2, then y = 1−i.
glossary.note: A short has zero impedance and no finite reciprocal admittance.

glossary.definition: For normalized impedance z with z ≠ −1, the Smith coordinate Γ = (z−1)/(z+1). For finite passive loads with nonnegative resistance, |Γ| ≤ 1. Its magnitude measures mismatch relative to the declared positive real reference resistance.

The fractional-linear coordinate map Γ = (z−1)/(z+1) and its inverse z = (1+Γ)/(1−Γ), on their stated domains. It takes the open positive-real half-plane to the open unit disk and finite purely reactive impedances to its boundary.
glossary.quick_example: The matched point z = 1 maps to Γ = 0. The point Γ = 1 has no finite impedance under the inverse formula.
glossary.note: Other literature uses different Cayley-transform conventions. Keep this direction and reference normalization explicit.

glossary.definition: A load with impedance equal to the chosen reference resistance in this real-reference model. Its normalized impedance is z = 1 and its reflection coefficient is zero. Matching is relative to the reference and frequency being used.
glossary.quick_example: A 50-ohm resistor is matched to a 50-ohm real reference and gives VSWR 1.

glossary.definition: For reflection magnitude r with 0 ≤ r < 1, VSWR = (1+r)/(1−r). The matched case gives one; as r approaches one the ratio diverges. The ideal passive boundary is assigned infinite VSWR.
glossary.quick_example: Reflection magnitude 1/3 gives VSWR 2.

glossary.definition: For 0 < |Γ| ≤ 1, the quantity −20 log₁₀|Γ| in decibels. Smaller reflected magnitude gives larger return loss. The matched limit |Γ| = 0 has ideal infinite return loss; the passive boundary |Γ| = 1 gives zero decibels.
glossary.quick_example: For |Γ| = 1/√5, return loss is 10 log₁₀5, approximately 6.99 decibels.

glossary.definition: In the guide’s propagation convention, a line of length ℓ gives Γin = ΓL exp(−4πiℓ/λ) at wavelength λ. It rotates the reflection point while preserving its magnitude. This is a physical line model with its own length and reference assumptions.
glossary.quick_example: A quarter wavelength multiplies Γ by −1 and sends a finite nonzero normalized load z to 1/z.
glossary.note: Line rotation alone cannot turn a nonzero reflection magnitude into a matched load.

glossary.definition: Reachability by a fixed finite set of phase rotations Γ ↦ ωᴷΓ, where ω = exp(2πi/N), N > 0 and K is an integer. For Γ₀ ≠ 0, a target Γ* is reachable exactly when (Γ*/Γ₀)ᴺ = 1. The zero start reaches only zero.
glossary.quick_example: For N = 4, the orbit of Γ₀ = 1/2 is {1/2,i/2,−1/2,−i/2}. A point at angle π/4 with radius 1/2 is outside this orbit.

glossary.definition: A point where a rational function has a nonremovable singularity after common factors are cancelled. A zero in a displayed denominator is only a candidate until cancellation is considered. Individual terms in a decomposition can have poles that cancel in their sum.
glossary.quick_example: The function 1/(1−t) has a pole at t = 1. By contrast, (1−t)/(1−t) extends to the constant 1 after cancellation.

glossary.definition: A quotient of polynomials over a declared field, understood with common factors cancelled when studying its poles or degree. In circuit work the variable is often complex frequency s. Frequency samples alone do not determine an arbitrary rational function without further constraints.
glossary.quick_example: The one-inductor example has normalized impedance z(s) = (7s+5)/(2s+4).

glossary.definition: In the real-rational scalar circuit setting, a rational function Z(s) analytic for Re s > 0 and satisfying Re Z(s) ≥ 0 there. Real coefficients give the usual conjugation symmetry. Boundary poles and realization restrictions require their stated additional conditions.
glossary.quick_example: For positive R and L, the series RL function Z(s) = R+sL has positive real part throughout Re s > 0.
glossary.note: Checking finitely many frequency samples is insufficient to establish positivity on the whole half-plane.

glossary.definition: A complex analytic function F on the open unit disk satisfying |F(t)| ≤ 1 throughout that disk. The Smith-chart research uses such reflection functions for interpolation. A rational Schur function has a finite rational description, with its degree and boundary behavior still to be specified.
glossary.quick_example: F(t) = t is a Schur function. It realizes the sample values 1/2 at t = 1/2 and −1/2 at t = −1/2.

glossary.definition: Finding a function in a declared class that takes prescribed values at prescribed nodes. Feasibility, uniqueness and the range of possible unmeasured values are separate questions. A fit in an unrestricted polynomial class need not satisfy the analytic or passive constraints of a circuit model.
glossary.quick_example: The data F(1/2) = 1/2 and F(−1/2) = −1/2 admit F(t) = t in the Schur class.

glossary.definition: For distinct disk nodes tₖ and proposed scalar values vₖ, the Hermitian matrix Pₖₗ = (1−vₖ conjugate(vₗ))/(1−tₖ conjugate(tₗ)). Its positive semidefiniteness is the classical scalar Schur interpolation criterion used in the linked reading.
glossary.quick_example: The nodes 1/2 and −1/2 with equal respective values give P = [[1,1],[1,1]], a rank-one singular matrix.
glossary.note: The nodes are distinct and strictly inside the disk. This criterion is not a component-count theorem for a restricted circuit topology.

glossary.definition: For Hermitian P ≥ 0, the block matrix [[P,b],[b*,d]] is positive semidefinite exactly when b is perpendicular to ker P and d ≥ b*P†b. Here P† is the Moore–Penrose inverse. The range condition remains essential when P is singular.
glossary.quick_example: If P = 0, its range is {0}. Positivity of the augmented block forces b = 0 as well as d ≥ 0.
glossary.note: Substituting a pseudoinverse into the scalar inequality while omitting the range condition is insufficient.

glossary.definition: For a proper scalar rational transfer function p(s)/q(s) in lowest terms, the degree of q. It counts the minimal state dimension of an unrestricted finite linear realization. Improper functions and restricted passive circuit component counts need their own conventions.
glossary.quick_example: The proper function (7s+5)/(2s+4) has no common numerator-denominator factor and has McMillan degree one.
glossary.note: A minimal state dimension does not alone give the minimum number of reactive elements in a transformer-free network.

glossary.definition: A network built from the allowed components whose driving-point impedance or transfer function equals the specified function on its stated domain. The component alphabet, positivity rules and permitted transformers determine the realization problem.
glossary.quick_example: The linked one-inductor example uses a series resistor 5/4 followed by a parallel resistor 9/4 and inductor 9/8 in normalized units.
glossary.note: An approximation by a lower-degree function is a realization of the approximating function. It does not establish an exact lower-component realization of the target.

glossary.definition: A description of a discrete linear system by xₙ₊₁ = Axₙ+Buₙ and yₙ = Cxₙ+Duₙ. It declares the retained state x, input u and observation y. Different coordinate systems can describe the same input-output behavior.
glossary.quick_example: The hidden-memory example has full state (y,z) and autonomous update matrix [[1,1],[1,0]]. Its visible observation selects y.

glossary.term: State sufficient for a deterministic update
glossary.definition: A retained value that determines its own next value for every admissible full state, under a specified deterministic evolution. If R is the summary and T the full update, this requires a map T̄ with T̄R = RT on the admissible states.
glossary.quick_example: In the Fibonacci update, y alone is insufficient, while (yₙ,yₙ₋₁) has the autonomous rule (u,v) ↦ (u+v,u).
glossary.note: Stochastic Markov properties concern conditional distributions and require their own probability model.

glossary.definition: An input x satisfying T(x) = x for a declared map T. For a linear projector P, the fixed points are precisely its image. Being fixed is an algebraic property; stability under nearby perturbations is a further question.
glossary.quick_example: The projector P(x,y) = (x,0) fixes every point on the horizontal axis.

glossary_comparisons.distinction: Seed rank counts generators under the declared operator action. Vector-space dimension counts basis vectors under scalar linear combinations. In the two-dimensional seed example, seed rank is one.
A projector satisfies P² = P. Orthogonality additionally depends on an inner product; algebraic packet reconstruction also permits oblique projectors.
SA = I recovers original objects after analysis. A two-sided inverse also satisfies AS = I on the coordinate space. Redundant coordinates can have the first identity without the second.
For a linear map, the kernel is the fiber over zero. Every nonempty fiber is a translate of that kernel. Fibers of a general nonlinear map need not have this form.

A residual records a discrepancy for the stated calculation. An obstruction rules out a proposed construction under specified assumptions. A nonzero residual alone need not rule out a different construction.
Arithmetic precision counts significant digits in a representation. A precision matrix is an inverse covariance. The shared word refers to different objects.
Exhaustive checking can prove a statement about its declared finite domain. Sampled cases in a larger domain require an additional argument to establish a universal statement.

A coordinate change sends vectors from x to y = Cx. Under that convention, the same operator T has matrix CTC⁻¹ in the y coordinates. Both the vector and operator descriptions must follow the declared direction.
An intertwiner C satisfies CT = UC and can be noninvertible. When C is invertible, this identity gives the conjugation U = CTC⁻¹.
Support records where a module remains nonzero after localization. In Q[t]/(tᵏ), every positive k gives the same support {(t)}, while k records the different module lengths and rational dimensions.

An inclusion-minimal certificate cannot be made smaller while remaining valid. A least certificate must be contained in every valid certificate for the same request. Incomparable minimal certificates can exist without a least one.
Least compares certificates by inclusion. Minimum cost compares their declared numerical costs. The shared-premise example has two minimum-cost certificates and no least certificate.

Free linear repair allows added directions chosen freely over the stated field. A finite repair menu restricts the choices to supplied candidates, with their costs and selection rules. Their minima answer different problems.

Reconstruction components SEᵢA sum to the identity when the coefficient selectors partition all coordinates and SA = I. In a redundant system, individual components need not satisfy Cᵢ² = Cᵢ. A projector must satisfy that extra identity.

A*A acts on the original vector space and measures the frame analysis. AS acts on coefficient space and projects onto valid analyzed coordinates. The reconstruction identity is SA = I, a third map with a different role.

Spectral radius uses eigenvalue magnitudes. An induced norm measures the largest one-step gain over all directions. The nilpotent matrix [[0,M],[0,0]] has spectral radius zero and Euclidean operator norm M.

Strong convergence follows each fixed input. Operator norm convergence controls all unit inputs uniformly. The first-m-coordinate projections on ℓ² converge strongly to I while their operator norm distance from I stays one.

An ordinary generating function stores aₙ against zⁿ. An exponential generating function stores aₙ against tⁿ/n!. Multiplication therefore uses ordinary coefficient convolution in the first convention and binomial convolution in the second.
A reciprocal solves A(t)B(t) = 1 and needs a nonzero constant coefficient over a field. A substitution inverse solves A(B(t)) = t and needs zero constant coefficient with nonzero linear coefficient.
Bell numbers count partitions into unordered blocks. Fubini numbers count the same partitions with their blocks linearly ordered. The factor k! records the possible orders of k blocks.

A residue coefficient selector retains named basis positions and is defined over any commutative ring. Roots-of-unity averaging realizes that selector over a field with the required primitive root and invertible modulus.

An analytic budget bounds the stated approximation steps. A directed numerical enclosure must also control finite arithmetic and outward rounding. A small analytic bound alone does not certify the computed endpoints.
A square orthogonal or unitary matrix is a surjective isometry. A rectangular isometric embedding preserves lengths but can leave part of its codomain unattained.

Eigenvalues describe scalar action on invariant directions of a square operator. Singular values describe nonnegative gains through A*A and also apply to rectangular maps. A nonzero nilpotent matrix can have only zero eigenvalues and a positive singular value.
The induced Euclidean norm is the largest singular value. The Hilbert–Schmidt norm is the square root of the sum of their squares. For diag(3,4), these norms are 4 and 5.
A real inner product is a symmetric positive definite bilinear form. Bilinearity alone allows indefinite or degenerate forms. Complex inner products instead use conjugate linearity in one argument.
Absolute error uses the output’s units. Relative error divides by a specified nonzero reference size. Near a zero target, the same absolute error can give a large or undefined relative error.
Forward error asks how far the computed answer is from the exact answer. Backward error asks how much permitted input data must change to make the computed answer exact. Conditioning links the two.

Formal series support coefficientwise algebra without numerical evaluation. A radius of convergence belongs to an analytic evaluation problem. A formal identity alone does not supply a truncation-error bound at a chosen argument.
The forward difference is f(x+1)−f(x); the backward difference is f(x)−f(x−1). On x² they give 2x+1 and 2x−1. Direction and step belong to the definition.
The falling product decreases successive factors by one, while the rising product increases them. The symbol (a)ₙ is convention-dependent, so compare the displayed product before using a formula.
A common phase on the whole state cancels in its density matrix. A phase difference between components remains in off-diagonal entries and can change interference measurements.
A measurement effect satisfies 0 ≤ E ≤ I. A projective effect also satisfies E² = E. The valid effect I/2 is not a projector.
Selective measurement retains the outcome and conditions the state on it. Coordinate dephasing discards that outcome and sums the branches, deleting the cross-coordinate coherence.

The line model uses a continuous physical length at a stated wavelength. A fixed order-N cyclic action permits only N phase rotations. Both preserve reflection magnitude, but their allowed phases differ.

Positive semidefinite Pick data decide feasibility in the stated scalar Schur interpolation problem. They do not alone decide realizability with a restricted transformer-free topology or a specified reactive-element count.
A necessary condition must hold for every solution. A sufficient condition guarantees a solution or property. A condition is both only after both implications are established.

An admissible counterexample disproves its stated universal claim. An inconclusive search has established neither a witness nor a proof of nonexistence. Rejecting one proposed witness can still leave many valid ones.
